A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Heise, A. M., & Wiessinger, D. (2011). Dysphoric milk ejection reflex: A case report. International Breastfeeding Journal, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/1746-4358-6-6

#6450. The 8 Best RV Generators Give You Go-Anywhere Power

Having the juice to power your appliances and electronics makes a mobile home feel truly homey.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Driving an RV lets you bring the comforts of home along on your road trip, but having a portable generator is essential. It powers your electric appliances and charges electronics, like your phone and laptop. If your RV doesn’t come equipped with a built-in generator, then you’ll need to bring one along.

To be clear: There are no official, task-specific “RV generators,” but some portable generators are better-suited to the task than others. For starters, most RVs have a 30-amp (A) outlet that lets you provide power to your entire RV, charging its batteries while running everything from lights to the air conditioner. The best RV generators need to be fairly beefy–powerful enough to keep multiple appliances running with juice to spare–but also portable enough to pack and, often, move in and out of the RV door.

An RV generator is a big investment, but an important one. We’ll help you find the right option for your setup and walk you through the shopping process and recommend the best models we’ve found and tested. With our picks, you can keep the power flowing wherever you roam.

Looking for more backup power solutions? Here are our reviews of the best portable generators, the best solar generators, and the best home generators.

This rock-solid block of generator excellence from Champion is as perfect for RVing as it gets. Its 4,500-watt output is more than enough to run your entire RV, including the air conditioner. At the same time, it’s surprisingly quiet, clocking in at just 61 decibels—the same volume as a dishwasher.

While it’s heavy at just over 100 pounds, it's fairly compact—the size of a couple of car batteries—and an integrated handle and wheels make it fairly easy to move around. It offers up to 14 hours of runtime on a single tank of gas (2.25 gallons), and you can expand the power capabilities by pairing it with a compatible generator using an optional parallel kit.

Champion has a whole line of inverter generators, but we recommend this one because it features a remote starter with a range of up to 80 feet, which we appreciate when we don’t feel like messing around with a generator in the cold or dark.

The Wen DF360iX offers quite a bit of utility for an affordable price. For starters, there is the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane at up to 3,600 or 3,500 starting watts, respectively, and either 900 or 2,600 running watts. (Propane generates slightly less power than gas.) That’s enough electricity for small to mid-size RVs.

At 49 pounds, this generator's relatively lightweight, but it doesn’t cut back on ports to keep the price low. It has a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV, two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. It also has an auto-shutoff feature if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t be too noisy for public areas like a campground.

There are some drawbacks to a generator at this price range, however. The size of the gas tank may be a concern. If you’re using gas and need it to run overnight, you’ll need a generator with a larger tank. At just 1.5 gallons, you only get up to five hours of usage with a half-load runtime (though using a 20-pound propane tank as your fuel can get that up to 14 hours). But if all you need is something basic, this gives you what you need at a good price.

Previously, we recommended the Pro version of this power station—mainly because it was highly portable with wheels and a telescoping handle—but Jackery has since discontinued it. Its replacement, the HomePower 3000, isn't quite as easy to move around, but it makes up for it with more power: It can generate up to 3,600 watts for 3,072 watt-hours of power capacity, and uses a LiFePO4 battery, which is more efficient and longer-lasting than the previous model.

While the HomePower 3000 no longer has wheels, it does have handles and weighs just under 60 pounds. There are larger portable power stations out there, but many are even more cumbersome than this one, making them exponentially more painful to lug in and out of your RV’s storage area.

More importantly, when paired with a pair of 200-watt SolarSaga panels, you can recharge the station in around 9 hours under sunny conditions. Of course, it can also be pre-charged much faster using an AC outlet, but when using solar, you can take yourself off-grid for longer periods.

It’s got all the connections you’ll need to power your RV, including a 30-amp outlet, plus four AC outlets, a 12-volt receptacle, and four USB ports should you need them. Other nice features include an app that allows you to monitor its power levels and output from your phone, and a battery management system that protects the station from power surges, overcurrent, and even extreme temperature conditions.

Dual-fuel generators are very nice to have on an RV, because the two types of fuel work well in different scenarios: gasoline is easy to obtain just about everywhere you go, so it's great for long, isolated trips or living off-grid, but makes a lot of noise. Propane isn’t quite as accessible, but it allows your generator to run more quietly.

We like the GD400BN specifically because it's powerful, quiet, and portable. With its 4,000-watt output, it’s more than capable of powering your entire rig, with the air conditioner, but it’s built solid and weighs less than 50 pounds. Another plug or two would’ve been nice–its single AC outlet limits things a bit if you have any reason to plug in power tools or equipment. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator and comes at a decent price to boot.

At this point, the Honda EU2200i is nothing short of a campsite icon. You see them all the time at campsites, and with good reason: They are renowned for doing pretty much everything right.

Weighing in at just over 46 pounds and not much larger than a couple of stacked shoeboxes, this is about as portable as RV-capable generators get. It’s also one of the quietest options in its class, purring along at 47-58 decibels, or about the same volume as a normal conversation. Test Editor Brad Ford found the same thing in his testing, calling the EU2200i “remarkably quiet.”

“The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on,” he wrote in our guide to the best portable generators.

And its durability is outright famous: I have personally spent years on end bumping and bashing one all over the place, and it just won’t break.

The primary downside is its 2,200-watt outage, which makes sense for its size but is relatively small if you’re powering an RV. Still, given how often you see it around, RVers are clearly okay working around its limitations.

I can report firsthand that the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra is an absolute performance monster, with massive output (7,500 watts) and enormous capacity (6,500 watt-hours), which you can expand further by adding extra 6,000-watt-hour batteries.

I recently had one along for a cloudy camping trip where solar panels would have been useless, but it didn’t matter because its charge lasted a solid three days (though it was cool weather and I wasn’t using my a/c—for that you’ll need solar). It also charges very quickly: I charged mine via a wall outlet in about 2 hours. I could easily use this generator to back up my entire house, so needless to say, it can store and produce enough energy to handily power an a/c and everything else you may need in your RV—particularly with a good solar setup.

The downside to carrying a generator like this around, of course, is the weight. At just over 180 pounds, it’s way too heavy to move in or out of an RV solo. It’s more portable than you might think, though: You can remove the batteries from the generator, then carry it out in more manageable parts. Plus, the power station has wheels to help you move it around. Ultimately, the Delta Pro Ultra is probably overkill for most RVers, but it pushes the boundaries on what you can expect from an RV-compatible generator.

When we tested the Bluetti Elite 300, we were impressed that this compact station boasted an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper. It’s not quite enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

We were also pleased with its solar recharging capability. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. It worked well when we paired it with a 250-watt portable panel.

The only thing we didn’t like was the inability to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 delivers a lot of power and runtime, but is still very portable and easy to store in an RV.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

If you want to be a good neighbor at your campsite, this generator from Westinghouse keeps the rumble to a minimum. Thanks to a special throttling system that only produces as much power as needed, it spins down when you aren’t drawing much rather than constantly roaring at full speed. That keeps the volume down, dropping to a decibel level akin to generators half its size at low usage. I’ve used older versions of what were essentially the same model; they were very quiet then, and reviews indicate the volume has gone down even more.

Its hefty 4,500-watt output is substantial, considering the lack of racket, and capable of powering an entire RV without issue. It also has a remote starter, which allows me to fire it up from the comfort of indoors.

This Westinghouse is fairly heavy, though a retractable handle, wheels, and lifting handles make it easier to move around. And its relatively compact shape passes through an RV door without too much trouble. All in all, it provides ample power while keeping the noise to a minimum.

We’ve used RV generators in all shapes and sizes for decades, and regularly test new models from both top manufacturers and up-and-coming startups. Our current selections are the result of all that experience. To supplement that experience, we compared our findings against a variety of expert reviews and those from real-world buyers at retailers like Amazon.

The recommendations below span a range of price points, portability, and operating specs, and situational needs, and after much testing and consideration, we are confident that these are truly some of the best RV generators you can buy right now.

Size matters–in watts (W), that is. Though power needs of RVs can vary widely, we generally suggest that most RVs need at least 2,000 watts at any given time—enough to power an air conditioner, fridge, lights, and a few devices. However, with just 2,000 watts, you’ll have to be careful about running the a/c along with other appliances, or you might run out of power quickly. If you’re spending a fair amount of time inside and plan to use your a/c often, look for a larger generator that can put out upwards of 3,500 watts.

If you’re using a solar generator (i.e., a power station connected to solar panels), you also need to consider your generator’s capacity, or its ability to store energy that’s been harnessed by a solar panel. To power an RV, you should look for a power station that can store at least 3,000 watt-hours (Wh), which is enough to power a fridge, lights, devices, and small appliances for a couple of days. And it needs to have an output of at least 2,000 watts, which allows it to power said essentials simultaneously.

Keep in mind that solar generators generally cannot generate as much juice as gas or a direct electrical hookup. Unless you have an extraordinary solar panel array and perfect sun to keep the power flowing, you probably won’t be able to power a full suite of appliances on solar alone.

Many RV generators run on gasoline, but there are also dual-fuel generators that allow you to use gas or propane. The advantage of propane is that it can run for longer when using, for example, a 20-pound tank (sometimes twice a long as the gas tank). It will also allow the generator to run more quietly. The disadvantage of propane is that it will deliver slightly less wattage.

A solar generator, a battery-based power station that you can recharge using a set of solar panels, is an increasingly popular and attractive option as well. You’ll need both to harness the power of the sun. While it takes time to fully charge a power station via solar panels, they’re more sustainable and work well if you’re camping off-grid. Plus, if you need to charge it in a hurry, all power stations can recharge by plugging them into a wall outlet.

Remember: It is never safe to run a gas or propane generator inside your RV. They emit carbon monoxide, which is deadly when allowed to build up indoors. Power stations, however, are safe to use indoors.

In addition to the standard 30-amp/120-volt outlet that you want to properly hook up your RV, the best RV generators will have a variety of plugs that will allow you to power or charge other devices directly. We usually look for standard AC outlets, like you’d find at home, which come in handy for plugging in power tools, outdoor appliances, or whatever else. Many generators also come with USB-A and USB-C ports to charge laptops, phones, and other tech.

If you plan on running everything off your RV, port variety may not be as important. But it’s a very nice value add if you plan to use the generator away from your RV.

Since any RV enthusiast is bound to find themselves in a campground or RV park during their travels. The locations often have rules around noise levels and won’t allow noisy generators to bother other guests. The National Park Service, for example, prohibits “operating motorized equipment or machinery that exceeds a noise level of 60 decibels.” This is based on a range of 50 feet. That gives you a little wiggle room, but we recommend 65 decibels or lower.

Traditional, fuel-based generators are often louder than this, so for RV use, we recommend using inverter generators. Not only do these run much quieter, but they provide more stable current, which is important if you are powering sensitive devices such as TVs, laptops, and microwaves. Meanwhile, power stations run virtually silently, so noise level is never an issue for them.

There’s no “set it and forget it” RV generator: You will need to move it around often, so it needs to be light enough for one to two people to carry in and out. In general, lighter is better, but we’d generally look for one around 40-50 pounds for a 2,000-watt generator, or 50-100 pounds for 3,000-4,000 watts. Some generators feature built-in wheels and handles, which makes life easier when moving them around.

All this moving also means the generator needs to be durable enough to take a few bumps here and there. Plus, you want it to last as long as possible without needing repairs. It’s hard to gauge durability on spec, but certain brands have reputations for strong build quality and sturdy construction. Even then, it always pays to look at user reviews and find out if your pick has a reputation for holding up over time.

Portable gas generators run anywhere from 6 to 18 hours, depending on their fuel capacity. When properly well-maintained, you should be able to run it until the tank runs dry, fill it back up, then start over. Never attempt to refill the gas tank while the generator is running, which can lead to fires.

Power stations, sometimes referred to as solar generators, can run for several hours to several days, depending on the capacity of the battery and how much power you are using. Once depleted, the battery can take 1-2.5 hours to recharge using AC power, or 9 or more hours using solar panels.

Various experts recommend that fuel-based (gas and propane) generators be placed anywhere from 5-25 feet away from the RV or home, but we’ve found that 5-10 feet is about right. Just make sure the generator is clear of doors and windows. You don’t want to run the risk of carbon monoxide blowing into the RV. Also, it shouldn’t push up against a wall or other gear–you’re your generator well-ventilated on all sides.

Because they don’t emit any exhaust fumes, power stations can be set up wherever you like; however, if you are pairing them with solar panels, you’ll need them to be within cable distance of the panels, and your panels will need to be positioned to capture sunlight.

You can, but you shouldn’t. Electricity and water don’t mix, and running a generator in the rain can have unpredictable results. At best, it may fry the generator or your RV electrical system. At worst, it could cause a fire or electrocute someone.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6449. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

D. Maity et al. Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity. Science. 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.ady8560

D. Maity et al. Blood‐glucose‐powered metabolic fuel cell for self‐sufficient bioelectronics. Advanced Materials. 2023. doi: 10.1002/adma.202300890

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

#6447. The 7 Best Standing Desk Chairs to Keep You Comfortable All Day Long

Take a break from your standing marathon with one of these stylish and functional seats.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Standing desks have become a go-to upgrade for anyone who works from home. Swapping your desk chair for a standing desk seems like an easy fix for a day spent slouched over a laptop, but standing still and upright for hours isn’t much healthier than sitting all day.

A 2024 study from the University of Sydney found that standing more didn’t lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, or heart failure, and it was linked to a higher risk of circulatory problems like varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis. To get the most out of your standing setup, you also need to sit for parts of the day.

If you work at a bar countertop or have a standing desk that can’t be lowered, a standard desk chair won’t work. The solution is an adjustable desk chair made for higher surfaces. It’s there when you need a break, and it’s easy to roll or slide out of the way when you’re ready to stand again.

For more great additions to your home office, check out our picks for the best WiFi mesh systems, best paper shredders, and our home innovation awards.

Most standing desk chairs are labeled as drafting chairs or task chairs, so we researched both for the best options. We consulted consumer reviews for insight into the types of chairs people enjoy, and scoured online retailers for high-quality options that will last. We prioritized decent adjustability, comfortable seats, and ergonomic shapes that suit a standing desk workspace.

If you’re looking for a standing desk chair that doesn't sacrifice style, then this drafting chair could be the perfect fit. It comes in seven colors to match any interior design scheme and adjusts up to 33 inches in height to fit any standing desk setup.

Both the seat cushion and back are padded for all-day comfort, and the armrests offer extra support when you need it. The attached footrest is also a great place to cool your heels when you want to kick back, relax, and unwind from standing at your desk all day.

If you’re looking for a chair for your standing desk but don’t want to break the bank, this is a great option. For just over $80, you’ll get an ergonomic and comfortable chair that can be adjusted up to 33 inches to reach the highest desks. The back height and seat depth are great for extended sitting, and the adjustable footrest provides extra support.

When you're not using it, you can lower it and store it under your standing desk.

Our pick for the best mesh standing desk chair is this Hylone model. What makes it so great is that every part is adjustable: the height, foot ring, and arms can all be customized to suit your comfort and needs.

This swivel drafting chair raises up to 31.2 inches to reach some of the highest desks, and its footrest adjusts to relieve pressure on your legs after hours of standing. The padded armrests add extra comfort if you need to sit back, relax, and unwind after a long day.

If you catch yourself leaning back in this chair, the breathable mesh keeps you from overheating while you take a break.

While searching for the best chair for your standing desk, you can't go wrong with a classic like this one from Modway. This model is sleek, adjustable, and ergonomic, and will give you some much-needed relief after working and standing all day. With the pull of a lever, the chair can be quickly raised from 21.5 inches to 29.5 inches.

The breathable mesh back, paired with lower-back lumbar support, is a must-have for anyone who needs extra comfort when they sit down. Better yet, despite this chair's long list of standout features, it will set you back just over $160 as of this writing.

Steelcase is known for its ergonomic gaming and office chairs, and interior designers praise its level of customizability. If you’re looking for a design that’s best for you, you can customize the Series 2 Stool's frame and seat colors, plus add an optional headrest, adjustable lumbar and arms, and carpet-compatible wheels.

The Series 2 Stool has a highly flexible seat that supports posture changes instantly. The brand recommends this stool for counter and bar-height tables, while its height adjustment and weight capacity are the most generous on this list. Steelcase also has an impressive 12-year warranty that covers part repairs and replacements.

If you're looking for a standing desk chair that's as attractive as it is comfortable, look no further than this padded faux-leather drafting chair from Markece. It is ergonomically designed with a padded backrest and seat cushion for ideal lumbar support, so your back will feel relieved after hours of standing at your desk.

And, if you have an extra-high desk, the seat on this chair can be raised nearly 36 inches above the chair's base.

Modernists and minimalists alike will love this chair. It’s the perfect balance of style and function, and it can fit well in any space. If your perfectly curated standing desk setup needs a chair, this one raises up to 34 inches. And if you want it out of sight when you're not using it, you can lower it and store it under the desk.

What’s even better is that this chair has lumbar support, so it can improve your posture—and keep you comfortable—if you sit in it for a while after standing.

To rest your legs and feet, you need a chair that reaches the right height, supports your feet when you’re seated, and gets out of the way when it’s time to stand.

Measure from the floor to the top of your desk at your usual standing height, then subtract 10 to 12 inches. That’s roughly the seat height you want, leaving room for your thighs under the desk. For a 42-inch desk, look for a seat that reaches 30 to 32 inches. Product listings usually give the seat height at its lowest and highest settings, and our picks top out anywhere from 29.5 inches to 35.8 inches.

At drafting height, your feet won’t reach the floor. Without something to rest them on, your legs dangle, and pressure builds up behind your thighs, which defeats the purpose of sitting down. Look for a foot ring or footrest, ideally one that adjusts, so your knees sit at a comfortable angle.

A backless stool keeps your core engaged and tucks under the desk when you aren't using it, so it's a good choice for small spaces. A chair with a backrest and lumbar support lets you fully rest, which matters more if you plan to sit for longer stretches. Armrests add comfort but can bump the edge of a high desk, so flip-up or removable arms are the most flexible.

Faux leather and vinyl are easy to wipe clean and usually cost less. Mesh breathes better if you run warm, and molded polypropylene or plastic seats are the lightest and easiest to move around. Check the weight capacity too. Our picks range from 250 to 400 pounds. And because you'll be moving the chair aside every time you stand, a lighter frame or smooth-rolling casters make the switch easier.

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

#6444. Menopause leaves clues in the blood about women’s future brain health

Blood protein changes around menopause may offer clues to later brain aging and Alzheimer’s risk, a new study suggests.

Menopause marks the end of a woman’s menstrual periods, often accompanied by hot flashes and disrupted sleep.

Changes in blood proteins may also offer clues to brain health decades later.

Compared with women who hadn’t reached menopause, those past it had more of certain proteins tied to inflammation, brain cell signaling, and Alzheimer’s disease.

That difference followed hormone levels more closely than age.

The same protein pattern appeared again in older women. Those whose blood showed it more strongly tended to decline faster on memory and thinking tests.

In the largest group, they also had a modestly higher risk of Alzheimer’s dementia.

Menopause may be a window for spotting the earliest signs of brain aging, years before memory problems usually appear.

The work was led by Madeline Wood Alexander at Sunnybrook Research Institute in Toronto, with Rowan Saloner and Kaitlin Casaletto at the University of California, San Francisco.

Because the findings come from blood samples and health records, they link these proteins to brain aging without showing that one causes the other.

“Menopause is not an isolated reproductive event,” said Emily Jacobs, a professor of psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara, whose lab runs the study that supplied the midlife volunteers.

“It is a whole-body biological transition. Now we can begin to see a molecular fingerprint of that transition in the blood and ask how it relates to brain health decades later.”

Menopause arrives around age 51 on average, more than two decades before dementia symptoms usually show up.

But the brain changes behind Alzheimer’s seem to start long before symptoms do, possibly around the same years as menopause.

The midlife part of the study included 80 healthy women aged 43 to 58. Thirty of them hadn’t reached menopause, 26 were in the transition often called perimenopause, and 24 had already passed through it.

In blood drawn after an eight-hour fast, the team measured about 120 proteins thought to be involved in brain aging. Sixteen of them were higher in women past menopause than in women who hadn’t reached it.

Eight of those 16 are involved in inflammation, four in the connections between nerve cells, and two in metabolism. The remaining two are tied to Alzheimer’s.

One is p-tau231, a form of tau, the protein that forms tangles inside brain cells in Alzheimer’s. The other is BACE1, an enzyme that helps make amyloid, the sticky protein in Alzheimer’s plaques.

The team also checked six standard Alzheimer’s blood markers. Once age was taken into account, p-tau231 was the only one that differed between women before and after menopause.

Next, the researchers combined the 16 proteins into a single score. It was lowest in women before menopause, higher in women in the transition, and highest in women past it.

Older women in the midlife group also had higher scores. That link disappeared once menopause stage was taken into account.

Thirty-six men of similar ages also gave blood, and in them the score didn’t rise with age at all.

Estradiol, the main form of estrogen, was about one-tenth as high in women past menopause as in women who hadn’t reached it.

Follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, was about nine times higher. The pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases FSH to signal the ovaries.

When estradiol, FSH, and progesterone were analyzed together, FSH was the only one still tied to the protein score.

Higher FSH was associated with higher levels of BACE1 and two proteins tied to nerve cell connections, while lower estradiol was associated with higher levels of four inflammation proteins.

The authors wrote that FSH receptors are common in brain regions that Alzheimer’s damages. In experiments on mice, FSH can trigger Alzheimer’s-like brain changes and thinking problems.

To check the results, the team turned to the UK Biobank, which holds health data from about half a million volunteers in the United Kingdom.

They compared 1,407 women past menopause with 1,407 women who hadn’t reached it, all aged 45 to 60 and matched closely on age.

In those women, a different lab method measured 2,923 proteins, and about 44% of them differed between the two groups.

The larger analysis measured 13 of the original 16 proteins. Nine showed differences in the same direction as in the midlife volunteers.

The team also used aging clocks, computer models that estimate how old an organ looks from blood proteins tied to that organ.

On 11 of 13 organ measures, women past menopause looked biologically older than women of the same age who hadn’t reached it.

The arteries, brain, and intestine showed some of the largest differences.

Among the midlife women in or past the transition, those who’d had night sweats in the previous two weeks had higher protein scores. They also had higher levels of four inflammation proteins.

Hot flashes, the sudden waves of heat many women feel around menopause, weren’t linked to the score in this group.

Women with vaginal dryness had lower scores, and the authors wrote that the meaning of that result is unclear.

Next came 89 older women, around 69 years old on average, from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer’s Prevention, which enrolls many people with a parent who had Alzheimer’s.

Those who reported a history of hot flashes or sleep problems had higher protein scores years after menopause.

One inflammation protein, CCL2, was tied to heat symptoms in both groups: night sweats in the midlife women and hot flashes in the older ones.

CCL2 helps call immune cells to sites of inflammation, and the authors wrote that its link to heat symptoms may last into later life.

The team then calculated the protein score for 11,925 older women in four separate groups, with average ages between about 61 and 72.

In a long-running Alzheimer’s study, 673 women around 71 years old were followed for about five years. Those with higher scores declined faster on memory and thinking tests.

The same was true in a smaller San Francisco study that followed 100 women for nearly six years.

The two groups started out very differently. More than half the women in the first study already had mild thinking problems or dementia at the start. Almost none in the San Francisco group did.

In the Wisconsin group, women with higher scores did worse on thinking tests taken at a single visit.

The UK Biobank group was the largest, with 11,059 women followed for nearly 16 years.

During that time, 219 of them developed Alzheimer’s dementia, and women with higher scores had a modestly higher risk of it. The scores weren’t linked to dementia of all types combined.

“Midlife is a critical window for both men and women where we can really set up the brain to be more resilient or more vulnerable to dementia in later life,” said Casaletto, one of the study’s senior authors.

“For women, menopause may be this especially powerful time to intervene.”

“The findings do not mean that menopause causes Alzheimer’s disease,” Casaletto said.

Most women don’t develop Alzheimer’s, she added, and it’s still unclear what small midlife rises in Alzheimer’s-linked proteins mean for any one person.

The authors described the link to Alzheimer’s dementia as relatively small.

The individual proteins most strongly associated with cognitive performance also varied across the groups of older women.

The authors wrote that the overall pattern may matter more than any one protein.

The midlife group was small and mostly White, and symptoms were self-reported. Proteins in the blood can also come from organs throughout the body, not only the brain.

“Women spend roughly one third of their lives after the menopause transition, yet we know remarkably little about the biology connecting menopause to later-life brain health,” Jacobs said.

Each midlife volunteer gave blood only once, so the study compared different women at different stages.

The authors wrote that confirming these shifts will mean following the same women from before menopause to years after it.

Those studies would track hormones, proteins, symptoms, and thinking along the way.

They could also separate the part of the change that comes from hormones from the part that comes with age.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Medicine.

#6443. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6441. Nearly a billion people face heatwaves and wildfire smoke in the same year

Heatwave wildfire smoke days now reach about 916 million people a year, and the heaviest burden falls on countries rarely linked to fires.

Most research on overlapping heatwaves and wildfire smoke has focused on the United States.

A global analysis now shows that people in Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Malawi experience the most days each year when these hazards coincide.

Between 2000 and 2019, about 916 million people a year lived through at least one such day, and the number grew by 287 million every decade. The reason is mostly more heatwaves, not more smoke.

Yao Wu of Monash University‘s School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine led the count with Yuming Guo and Shanshan Li, in collaboation with researchers from Peking University and the University of Tasmania.

The team matched daily temperatures to estimates of fire smoke in the air, square by square, on a grid about 17 miles (28 kilometers) wide.

The researchers then overlaid population maps to estimate how many people were exposed.

Overlap days per person rose from 1.0 a year in the first decade to 1.7 in the second.

When the team split that growth into its parts, 70.5 percent came from people living through more overlap days and 29.5 percent from population growth.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wu explained what that increase means.

“In other words, the problem is growing mainly because people are experiencing these two hazards together more frequently, not simply because there are more people,” Wu said.

Heat explains most of that. Heatwave days increased in 87 percent of the squares on the map, but smoke days increased in only 28 percent of them, mostly in North America.

So a larger share of smoky days now coincides with a heatwave, while the share of heatwave days that also carry smoke has barely moved.

The two hazards also showed a clear timing pattern.

Across the globe, the chance of a smoke episode starting began to climb about two days before a heatwave began, and it peaked on the heatwave’s first day.

A smoke day, in this count, was any day when fine particles or ozone in the air exceeded the World Health Organization’s daily guideline.

At least half of that pollution had to come from landscape fires, a category that includes forest fires, grassland fires and the burning of crop waste.

A heatwave meant at least two consecutive days with temperatures above the local 90th percentile – hotter than 90 percent of days in the reference period.

That is the most lenient common definition, and the team chose it to catch as many hot days as possible.

Africa accounted for about 39 percent of all person-days of overlap, with one person-day representing one person exposed for one day.

People in low-income countries averaged 4.4 overlap days a year, against 0.4 in high-income countries.

That gap widened over the two decades, because the low-income countries also had the fastest increase.

Five countries accounted for half of all person-days between 2010 and 2019: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

A different pattern emerged when the team compared annual exposure per person.

Zambia ranked highest that decade, averaging 28.8 days a year, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 24.3 and Malawi at 21.7.

“These findings highlight that some of the countries experiencing the greatest exposure are not necessarily those receiving the most international attention for wildfires,” Wu told Earth.com.

Asked by Earth.com which country’s trend surprised the team most, Wu named Cambodia.

It ranked 40th in overlap days per person in the first decade, at 1.6 days a year, and ninth in the second, at 12.1 days.

“What makes this particularly noteworthy is that Cambodia experienced substantial economic growth during this period, yet exposure to these overlapping environmental hazards also increased sharply,” Wu said.

Economic development, Wu said, does not necessarily translate into less exposure.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo showed the largest absolute rise, from 11.8 overlap days per person a year to 24.3. Europe and Oceania saw slight declines that were too small to separate from chance.

Wu’s advice for such a day is to guard against both hazards at the same time.

Check the local heat and air quality warnings, limit outdoor activity and especially hard exercise, and stay somewhere cool with clean air.

Air conditioning and air filtration help, and so does drinking enough water.

“The challenge is that protective measures for heat and wildfire smoke can sometimes conflict,” Wu said. “For example, opening windows may help cool a home but can also allow smoke indoors.”

For a household with neither air conditioning nor a filter, Wu suggested shading the windows and cutting indoor heat sources.

Another option is a public space that offers both cooling and cleaner air. Older adults, children and people with existing health conditions may need particular attention, Wu added.

The study counted exposure, not illness. It did not track anyone’s health, so it reports how many people breathed smoke on a hot day and nothing about what happened to them afterward.

Earlier work suggests that heat and smoke together may do more harm than the two added separately.

The smoke figures are also estimates from a computer model of the atmosphere, checked against ground monitors where they exist.

The model handles the height of a smoke plume imperfectly, which can overstate pollution near a fire and understate it downwind. Carbon monoxide was left out of the count.

And the record stops at the end of 2019. Wu said the heatwaves and fires since then “raise concerns that combined exposure may have continued to increase, particularly in low-income countries,” but the team can’t yet put a number on it.

The next step is to use these maps to study how combined exposure affects health, especially in countries that have received little research attention.

The findings could also help shape warning systems that address heat and smoke together.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
