Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Lu, Y., Song, J., Chi, X., Li, W., Wu, L., Guo, Y., Cui, Q., Zheng, X., Bai, Y., Heng, B. C., Han, X., Zhang, X., & Deng, X. (2026). Self-charged toothbrush facilitates tooth healthcare maintenance. Science Advances, 12, Article eaeg5744. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg5744

Isha Ishtiaq is a freelance health journalist based in Pakistan who covers health, medicine and biomedical research. Her work has appeared in Live Science, Science News, and Medscape, among other outlets. She holds a B.S. (Hons) in biotechnology from the University of Gujrat and an M.S. in biological sciences from the University of Sialkot, where her research focused on the use of deep learning models for disease detection.

#6439. Planting billions of trees is harder than climate pledges make it sound

Poverty, hunger, and insecure land rights could limit efforts to plant new forests and remove carbon from the atmosphere, a global study finds.

Plant enough trees and they pull carbon out of the air, which is why most national climate pledges lean on new forests.

But planting forests takes money, secure access to land, and conditions that allow trees to survive.

A new global analysis shows how poverty, hunger, insecure land rights, and weak governance overlap with opportunities to remove carbon through new forests.

About 73% of that potential lies in countries facing medium-to-high social and economic barriers.

Wenkai Bao, a geographer in the Department of Geography at LMU Munich, led the study.

Julia Pongratz, a professor there who also works at the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology, is a co-author.

The analysis identifies patterns in where planted forests remain standing, but it does not establish what caused those differences.

Bao’s team began with more than 200 published case studies of tree-planting projects and pulled out ten things that kept getting in the way.

Then it built 78 machine-learning models to ask which of the ten best explained, country by country, how much planted forest is actually standing today.

Five economic factors accounted for about 69% of the combined importance assigned to the ten barriers.

Poverty came first, at a quarter of the total, and food insecurity second, at a fifth.

The cost of planting, the size of the forestry workforce and the state of forest roads trailed behind them.

Insecure land tenure and weak governance came next, at about 11% and 10%. Forest policy on its own barely registered, at 4%.

More policies did not reliably mean more forest.

The relationship with poverty emerged only above a high threshold. Beyond that point, higher poverty was associated with less standing planted forest.

The models were run at the country level, because most social and economic data exist only that way.

The models assessed existing planted forests using four measures, including total area and the share of land physically suitable for forest growth that had been planted.

Of the 78 models, 27 explained at least half the variation between countries, and the team worked from those.

It then checked the results against swapped-in datasets and against planted forests that excluded commercial plantations, and the pattern held.

Common development scores did not work as substitutes.

When the team swapped in GDP per person or the Human Development Index for the tree-specific measures, the models got much worse at explaining where forests stood.

The team laid its constraint scores over existing maps of where new forests could remove the most carbon.

About 73% of that potential sat in countries with medium-to-high constraints, and so did about 70% of the highest-potential hotspots.

The split runs along the line between the Global North and the Global South.

Europe has few constraints and little room for new forest. The tropics, where Africa’s forests and the Amazon sit, hold most of the room and most of the constraints.

The promises already made under the Paris Agreement are where this matters.

The ten countries with the biggest tree-planting pledges account for nearly 90% of all pledged area, the authors wrote. Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Colombia face high constraints, with poverty as the main one.

India falls in the medium tier mainly because of food insecurity, while limited forest-road infrastructure is Canada’s main barrier.

In India, the authors wrote, decades of large planting programs have failed to raise canopy cover or help local livelihoods.

Pongratz said the stakes run through every net-zero plan.

“To reach greenhouse gas neutrality, we will have to at least triple the global amount of CO2 that we remove from the atmosphere by 2050,” she said.

“Additional forest cover will play the dominating role while we scale up technological removal options.”

The constraints don’t all pull the same way, and one example in the paper is Vietnam. Its poverty level is relatively high, yet it ranks among the countries with the most secure land tenure.

It has also planted and kept a large area of forest over recent decades, and the authors suggest the secure tenure is what made the difference.

Brazil shows the reverse, and it is not among the poorest countries.

When it relaxed its Forest Code and field enforcement fell away, carbon emissions from the Amazon rose sharply in 2019 and 2020, the authors wrote.

There is a cost to getting this wrong beyond lost carbon. In the case studies, failed projects took land from poor households without replacing their income.

In some places, people burned the planted area to be hired again for the replanting.

Bao put the prescription plainly. “Credible climate strategies must pair afforestation and reforestation with efforts that strengthen livelihoods, rights, and institutions,” Bao said.

The models find patterns, not causes. They were built on forests planted mostly for timber and conservation, because deliberate planting for carbon removal is still rare.

Carbon prices or changing diets could reshape the constraints in ways the data can’t show.

Success was measured as planted forest still standing. It wasn’t measured as carbon stored, wildlife returned or livelihoods improved, which the authors list as the next indicators to add.

And the overlay map shows where risks and potential coincide, not how much carbon is lost to them. It can’t say how much of the hoped-for carbon removal will fail to happen.

Tracking changes in planted forests alongside social and economic conditions could help researchers test which barriers directly affect planting success.

The full study was published in the journal One Earth.

#6437. Riskier decisions may offer an early warning of heavier drinking

Changes in phone game decisions predicted heavier drinking the following month in a yearlong study of people with alcohol use disorder.

Alcohol has a reputation for making people take risks. But a yearlong study of people with alcohol use disorder found that changes in decision making came before heavier drinking.

When participants took certain risks in phone games, they drank more the following month. Heavier drinking, however, did not predict riskier choices the next month.

The researchers tracked changes within each person rather than simply comparing heavier and lighter drinkers.

Most participants had mild or moderate alcohol use disorder, making them a potentially important group for early intervention.

Hilmar Zech, a postdoctoral researcher at University Hospital Würzburg and TU Dresden in Germany, led the study with Lorenz Deserno.

The team also included co-authors at Charité in Berlin and the Central Institute of Mental Health.

“This temporal direction was specific and was not observed vice versa, even after accounting for the amount of previous drinking,” Deserno said.

The researchers followed 603 people, ages 16 to 65, for one year. All of them met at least two of diagnostic criteria for alcohol use disorder.

In the study, a standard drink held 0.4 ounces (12 grams) of pure alcohol. The participants averaged about three of those a day, and about five on the days they drank.

Every two days, each person reported what they had drunk from a list of 19 options, from a small beer to a bottle of wine.

Every four weeks, they also played four five-minute games on their phones. In one game, fruit fell from a tree and the player tapped to collect it, unless the fruit turned brown.

In another, red circles flashed on a grid and the player had to remember their positions. Those two measured self-control.

The other two measured decision making. In a gambling game, the player chose between a sure amount and a coin flip, in versions built around wins, losses, or both.

In a card game, the player could pay to flip over cards before guessing which of two face-down rows added up to more.

The mixed version offered a possible win or a possible loss on the same flip. In months when a person took that gamble more often, that person drank more the next month.

The card game gave the same result. When someone flipped fewer cards before guessing, they drank more in the month that followed.

In the loss version, the link was reversed. In months when a person gambled more to avoid a sure loss, they drank less the following month.

Earlier studies had compared people with alcohol use disorder with people without it at a single point in time.

Those studies found a similar pattern: people with alcohol use disorder were more willing to gamble when both winning and losing were possible, but less willing when the gamble involved only potential losses.

As far as Zech’s team knows, no study had watched those shifts come and go inside one person and then watched the drinking follow.

“We found that monthly fluctuations in aspects of decision making predicted subsequent alcohol consumption,” Zech said.

Next the team ran the question backward. Did heavy drinking in one month change how a person played the games the next month?

The researchers found no evidence of that pattern.

The forward link also held after the team accounted for the fact that one month’s drinking resembles the last.

In a second analysis built for a year with many zero-drink days, the loss-version result held up, and the other two showed the same direction with more uncertainty.

The two self-control games did not follow that pattern.

A person’s monthly ups and downs in avoiding rotten fruit or remembering circles had no link to the drinking that followed.

Working memory still mattered, but between people instead of within one person.

Participants who could hold more circles in mind drank less on average over the year than participants who could hold fewer.

Cameron Carter, editor-in-chief of the journal that published the study, explained why experimental tasks matter.

“Decision making and cognitive control cannot be accurately examined through interviews or self-reports and instead require experimental tasks,” Carter said.

The effects were small. Zech’s team wrote that they are likely too small to be useful in a clinic yet.

The team had also planned to split the sample in two, with the second half meant to confirm what the first half found.

The pattern was clear in the first half and not in the second, although the two halves did not differ from each other when the team compared them directly.

The team also split the 603 people into random halves 1,000 times. The direction came out the same every time, and a group of about 300 was often too small to detect the effect.

Of the 603 who started, 218 dropped out early. Their data stayed in, and leaving was not tied to how they played or how much they drank.

The self-control games may simply have been played too rarely. A few studies that checked several times a day did find self-control dipping before drinking, though only under certain conditions.

Once a month may be too rare to catch that. And a study that watches people without changing anything can’t say that the risky choices caused the drinking.

Whether a game score can predict heavier drinking over the following week, rather than month, is still an open question.

The team envisions an app that flags changes in a person’s risk-taking score and offers automated support or prompts them to seek help in person.

Whether that approach would work remains untested.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging.

#6436. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6435. Quantum experiment reveals signs of long-predicted protected states

A tiny junction on a topological insulator seemed to close and reopen its energy gap, a key prediction of topological quantum computing.

A quantum computer’s biggest weakness is that its information is easily disturbed. One proposed fix is to store it in quantum states that are built to resist local disturbances.

Physicists in Germany have now seen signs of those states behaving the way a 2008 theory said they should.

The team detected the signals inside a junction just 50 nanometers wide, on a sliver of material that conducts electricity along its surface.

Earlier evidence in this kind of material was indirect, the authors wrote. This time, they directly measured the energy spectrum inside the junction.

Jakob Schluck and Ella Nikodem did the experiment in Yoichi Ando’s lab at the University of Cologne. Theorists in Fabian Hassler’s group at RWTH Aachen University ran the simulations.

Both groups belong to the ML4Q cluster, which works on quantum computing. What they saw fits the prediction, they wrote, but it isn’t yet proof of it.

“It is super exciting to see our experimental results align so well with theoretical predictions,” Nikodem said. “This is very encouraging in terms of future applications in quantum computing.”

The material is a topological insulator. It insulates on the inside and conducts along its surface.

On that surface, each electron’s spin is tied to its direction of travel, which helps protect it against being scattered straight backward.

Liang Fu and Charles Kane predicted in 2008 what would happen if a conventional superconductor were laid on top of such a surface.

The surface should become a new kind of superconductor, one that can host quantum states called Majorana zero modes.

Those modes are candidate building blocks for quantum bits that local disturbances can’t easily corrupt.

The theory makes a specific prediction for a junction between two superconductors on that surface.

As the difference between their superconducting phases reaches half a cycle, the energy gap inside the junction should close and then reopen.

The team made the junction from two strips of aluminum on a flake of the material BiSbTeSe2, 10 to 20 nanometers thick.

The strips end about 50 nanometers apart, roughly a thousandth of the width of a human hair. An aluminum loop connects them, so a tiny magnetic field sets the phase.

Two gold electrodes, separated from the junction by a thin oxide layer, probe the energies of the states inside it at different locations.

The device was cooled to 50 millikelvin, just 0.05°C above absolute zero.

With no magnetic field, the readout showed an energy gap, with two peaks at 130 microelectronvolts on either side of zero.

As the field tuned the phase toward the halfway point, the peaks slid inward and merged into one broad peak at zero. The gap appeared to close.

A stronger field reopened it, and the pattern repeated every 230 microtesla, which matched the device’s dimensions.

A conventional junction keeps its gap at that point unless its electrons pass through perfectly, the authors wrote, and a surface whose electrons can’t reverse guarantees exactly that.

Simulations of a simple model in Aachen reproduced the crossing.

The pattern held while the team swept a gate voltage from -20 to +20 volts, which shifted the surface electrons’ energy by at least 40 millielectronvolts. It also held in a second, nearly identical device.

In stronger fields of 5 to 6 millitesla, the closing showed up only at particular spots.

The theory says the field should pin the zero-energy state to points along the junction. The two electrodes saw the gap close at different times as those points moved past them.

“Understanding how superconductivity interacts with the distinctive electronic properties of topological insulators is essential for assessing their potential for topological quantum computing,” Ando said.

The experiment can resolve energies down to about 30 microelectronvolts, and a gap smaller than that would look closed.

Electrons passing through at 95% or better would produce what the team saw, by its calculation.

That makes topological protection a plausible explanation, the authors wrote, but leaves room for alternatives.

The authors also weighed two ordinary explanations. A stray state in the insulating layer produced a similar signal in one device, but only at a single gate voltage, unlike the stable pattern here.

Disordered junctions can close a gap through a few open channels, which the authors considered unlikely to hold up across such a wide gate sweep.

The predicted transition into a topological superconducting state has not yet been confirmed.

It would show up as a change in the junction’s parity, and charge sensing could detect that.

Higher-frequency measurements could sharpen the energy resolution.

The authors also calculated that niobium electrodes, which tolerate fields of around 100 millitesla, could hold well-separated Majorana modes.

“To demonstrate the topological phase transition in this system, we need to improve the experiment’s energy and time resolution – this is the next step on the roadmap of the Ando lab,” Schluck said.

Until then, the gap in this junction looks closed. Whether it truly closes is the question the next device has to answer.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Magma and a possible environment for ancient life might be present on Mars in the region of a large volcano on the Red Planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests.

Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars.

Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year. But the new findings are the strongest evidence yet of gases being released by dormant volcanoes on Mars, first study author Alexander Trokhimovskiy, at Russia's Space Research Institute, told Live Science.

"Our study offers a complementary and potentially independent line of evidence [of Martian magma]: Atmospheric observations that reveal a possible signature of gas release from a subsurface magmatic system," Trokhimovskiy wrote in an email.

TGO first detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars' atmosphere in 2021, but scientists were hesitant to link it to volcanic activity. The gas appeared to be seasonal, its distribution was not localized at a possible volcanic region, and other signs of volcanic gases, like sulfur, were not present, study co-author Kevin Olsen, a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford who studies Mars gases, told Live Science in a separate email.

A photo of Mars with the Tharsis region centered.

Further work, however, suggested that the gas wasn't just popping up in the warmer spring and summer in Mars' southern hemisphere; it also appeared in the winter in the northern hemisphere, he noted.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"I managed to catch two observations from the start of northern winter in the first Mars year of our mission, and a single observation the next year," Olsen said, adding that a year on Mars is closer to two years on Earth due to the planet's wider orbit. "These out-of-season measurements were close to one another in location and time in both years, which was rather surprising. We then set about creating a campaign of special, targeted measurements at this time and place."

That campaign lasted two Mars years — roughly four Earth years — and increased the likelihood that scientists are seeing "an injection" of hydrogen chloride into the atmosphere from volcano-adjacent vents, Olsen said.

The scientists confirmed the unseasonal observations in the northern hemisphere, finding a "distinct and pronounced signal" that then diminishes and falls below the spacecraft's detection threshold. "This inconsistency is more suggestive of a puff of gas entering the atmosphere than of regular atmospheric chemistry," he said. "While the link remains a hypothesis, we have now seen this gas appear locally, and nowhere else, over four Mars years of observations."

Daniel Mège, also a co-author of the paper and a professor who studies planetary geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, identified the fissures where the gas may be emerging. He said the complementary evidence from InSight (on the ground) and TGO (circling above) helps give the study weight: InSight spotted activity in the crust, while TGO detected the emissions in the atmosphere.

Although magma activity is not in itself a sign of life, Mège noted that Earth's first life-forms came from sites like hydrothermal zones, which have a similar confluence of materials and energy as the potential vents on Mars. But conditions would need to be favorable in that area for at least millions of years to allow life to form, he cautioned.

"If these requirements are met at local scale, at the scale of the seepage structures, then living organisms might wait for us to discover them," he told Live Science in an email. "But maintaining stable conditions over such a long period at a very local scale is not obvious."

#6432. Where does consciousness begin? A new theory points deep inside the brain

A brainstem theory of consciousness puts the raw feeling of being 'you' in the brain's ancient stalk, and its evidence starts with pain.

Consciousness is often linked to the cortex, the brain’s wrinkled outer layer, which helps us understand language, recognize faces, and make plans.

Yet a surgeon who stimulates that layer in an awake patient can reliably produce flashes of light, sounds and tingling, and almost never pain.

Two neuroscientists now propose that the raw feeling of being conscious, the “me inside,” is computed somewhere else.

Their candidate is the brainstem, the ancient stalk at the base of the brain. The case rests on pain, and it is a hypothesis built from existing evidence, not a new experiment.

The cortex, they propose, works out what you are seeing and hearing. A small region of the brainstem, they suggest, determines what you consciously feel.

Marshall Devor of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem laid out the argument with Mark Baron, a neurologist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.

Close your eyes and cover your ears, they wrote, and “you” are still there, 100 percent.

Electrical stimulation of the visual cortex during brain surgery makes patients see light. Stimulating the hearing and touch areas produces sounds and tingling.

The neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield wrote in the 1950s that only very rarely did a patient use the word pain to describe the result of cortical stimulation. His observation still holds, Devor and Baron wrote.

One exception is a buried cortical region called the insula.

In one study the authors cite, stimulating it evoked pain at only 8 of 313 sites tested. Painful auras are rare in epilepsy too, and pain rarely appears in dreams.

Damage points the same way. Lesions in the visual cortex cause blindness, but no cortical removal anywhere prevents pain from being felt, Penfield wrote.

If anything, the authors wrote, cortical strokes can add chronic pain rather than remove it. Yet those patients remain conscious.

Small strokes in specific parts of the brainstem can cause coma, the authors note.

Devor and Baron also point to adults with hydrocephalus who remained fully articulate despite extreme thinning of the cortex.

The authors’ own rat work narrows the spot. The team microinjected a a general anesthetic into rat brains 828 times, in 182 animals.

The drug knocked the rats out only when it landed in one small region of the brainstem, the mesopontine tegmentum.

Doses of 10 billionths of a liter or less worked within seconds, and injections slightly off target didn’t.

Destroying that small area alone did not cause coma, so the authors wrote that it isn’t the whole story.

Somewhat larger lesions centered on it did, in a region about an eighth of an inch (3 millimeters) by a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters). That region, they wrote, matches where strokes cause coma in people.

In the authors’ model, the cortex does the heavy processing: telling a rhinoceros from a cloud, or a snake in the grass from rustling leaves.

It also works out whether what it sees is good or bad for survival, and it sends that verdict down to the brainstem.

The brainstem circuit then determines which information enters awareness.

If the new input matters more than whatever “you” are attending to now, it marks that stream of cortical processing as conscious.

The rest keeps running unattended, like a self-driving car.

“We humans are sentient robots,” the authors wrote. Pain skips the round trip, because signals from nerve fibers that detect potentially harmful stimuli already flag a threat.

Devor and Baron also offer an evolutionary reason.

The mammalian neocortex had not yet evolved when fish and reptiles emerged, and the ability to feel pain, they propose, arose early as an add-on to escape reflexes.

In their account, the later evolution of the mammalian neocortex built on the brainstem’s existing machinery for conscious experience.

The brainstem theory of consciousness is a framework, not a mechanism.

Hundreds of theories of consciousness exist, the authors wrote, and none of them, their own included, explain how neurons produce subjective experience.

Devor and Baron claim only that the mechanism is biological and that it has one location.

Could a fish, a reptile, or even an invertebrate feel pain without a cortex? The authors suspect so but wrote that there is no sure way to know.

Researchers cannot directly confirm subjective experiences in people or animals unable to describe them. In the rats, the team measured anesthesia and sleep, not feeling.

Devor and Baron propose studying the mesopontine tegmentum and its connections directly.

The lab’s earlier work mapped which of that region’s neurons send axons up toward the cortex and down the spinal cord.

Whether any of those cells carry the signal that turns processing into experience is the question the theory leaves open.

The hypothesis was presented in the journal The Neuroscientist.

#6431. Researchers discover the clever tactics octopuses use to fit through holes much smaller than their bodies

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through a gap far narrower than its body. It often does that in the wild to escape predators and…

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through a gap far narrower than its body. It often does that in the wild to escape predators and to catch prey.

In a recent study, scientists have deciphered the exact, step-by-step method that common octopuses squeeze through tiny holes.

One arm goes through first. Several more follow, and then the arms that are already through push against the wall around the hole and pull the rest of the animal after them.

When the hole was narrower than the distance between an octopus’s eyes, the animals added a step: every arm went through before the head and body did.

Wenci Xin, a mechanical engineering researcher at the National University of Singapore, and colleagues filmed three common octopuses at a public aquarium in Vienna.

Then the team tracked every arm, frame by frame. The whole-body squeeze had never been broken into steps before, the team wrote.

The three were young animals, caught by fishermen at La Ciotat in France and kept at the Haus des Meeres, the Vienna aquarium. A clear acrylic wall with one adjustable hole split their tank.

An octopus has a capsule of cartilage around its brain, and the distance between its eyes is a good guide to how big that capsule is. So the team used that distance as each animal’s size.

The smallest octopus, with eyes 0.6 to 0.8 inches (15 to 20 mm) apart, got a hole about as wide as a penny, 0.8 inches (20 mm) across.

The two bigger ones, with eyes 1.2 to 1.4 inches (30 to 35 mm) apart, got a hole 1.2 inches (30 mm) across. That’s about the width of a soda bottle cap, and narrower than the distance between their eyes.

Each animal made three to five attempts a day on three separate days. If an octopus seemed unwilling to go on, or jetted water, a stress response, the team stopped and waited at least three days.

Cameras recorded 33 attempts. Three failed when the octopus damaged the apparatus trying to get out another way, which left 30.

Every squeeze started the same way. The octopus pushed one arm through the hole, bending it into a U at the opening. Then the arm stretched out on the far side.

Michael Kuba of the University of Naples Federico II, who helped run the new work, had seen that reaching move before. In a 2015 study, Kuba and colleagues filmed octopuses reaching one arm through a hole.

Next, more arms followed the first, with shorter reaches, until they filled the hole almost completely. The team calls that shifting. Three to five arms went through at this stage, and four was the most common number.

The last step was the squeeze itself. Two of the arms on the far side twisted around and attached their suckers to the wall. By stiffening and pushing against the wall, they pulled the remaining arms, the head, and the body through in one motion.

At the wider hole, that was the whole routine, and the smallest octopus used it in all 14 of its attempts.

The two bigger octopuses, with a hole narrower than the distance between their eyes, did something different at the last step.

First the octopus rotated its body upward, which forced the bases of the arms already in the hole deeper in and opened up a little more room.

The remaining arms then twisted and stretched through, with the arms on the far side pulling, until all eight arms were through.

Once the arms were across, the octopus turned back to its normal position, with only the head and body left on the starting side.

The second pull worked like the first one: two arms attached to the wall pushed against it, and this time only the head and body came through.

From the side, the cameras caught the body narrowing before it went through. The hole pressed the body narrower, and the octopus narrowed it further on its own, the team wrote.

Those two octopuses used this four-step version in 15 of their 16 attempts.

In an interview with Earth.com, Xin said the team had expected the same strategy at both hole sizes, with the arms pushing against the wall to pull the animal through.

“We were surprised when we found that the strategy changed,” Xin said. “However, after thinking about it carefully, we felt that it was understandable, as the animals were still following the same general pattern, while the new strategy simply divided the sequence in which the body was pulled through into separate stages.”

The octopuses favored their four front arms, and the two on the left most of all. Counting from the front, the second left arm went first in 47% of the 30 attempts, and the first left arm in another 28%.

The arms that followed were usually the ones next to the probing arm. At the wider hole, the two arms at the ends of that group consistently did the pulling.

At the narrower hole, when the second left arm had probed, the first right arm and the fourth left arm nearly always pushed the body through.

The team also tested four-month-old juveniles of a second species, the Mexican four-eyed octopus. Offered a hole 0.4 inches (10 mm) wide, no wider than the distance between their eyes, the young octopuses did not try it. Two Mexican four-eyed octopuses given a penny-wide hole used the three-step routine every time.

Offered a 0.6-inch (15 mm) hole beside two 0.4-inch ones, one animal tried a narrow hole first. It got one arm through, then two more, and could not get any more through. After several failed tries it moved to the wider hole and went through in three steps.

Robots built to search collapsed buildings have to fit through gaps in the rubble, so they’re built narrow, and a narrow body leaves little room for equipment, Xin said. Engineers make the robot longer instead, which is why so many rescue robots look like snakes.

“If we could develop a squeezable, octopus-inspired robot, such a design could accommodate a larger range of functional components while retaining access to confined spaces,” Xin told Earth.com.

Each of its eight arms could do the job of one slender rescue robot, carrying sensors, tools, or communication devices.

Cecilia Laschi of the National University of Singapore supervised the work. Laschi and Kuba co-wrote a 2015 paper on a soft eight-arm robot that moves and grasps underwater like an octopus. The hard part of a soft robot like that is control.

An octopus arm can bend anywhere along its length, so there’s almost no limit to the ways it can move. That makes it hard to control. So is a robot arm built the same way.

The authors suggest the octopus keeps control simple by reusing a few standard arm moves and organizing them into one motion.

The moves are a bend, a stretch, a twist, and a stiffening. The footage can’t prove it, they wrote, because the moves varied from one attempt to the next.

Each of the three octopuses was tested at only one hole size. So the authors can’t say whether the extra step came from the hole size or from the individual animal’s own preferences.

The octopuses’ preference for their left arms may come from the tank itself, the team wrote: one side of it gave the animals a clearer view out.

And the cameras were aimed at the arms and the head, not the body, so how much the body narrows to fit has not been measured.

The usual assumption has been that the beak sets the limit on how small a hole an octopus can get through.

The failed attempts suggest the limit may also depend on how thick all eight arms are together where they join the body. An octopus may not be able to tell whether it will fit before it tries.

Xin called the work an initial study with many open questions. “For example, can this behavior harm the animal, and what determines the smallest opening an octopus can squeeze through?” Xin explained.

The next step the authors propose is a larger group of octopuses, with each one tried at more than one hole size.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

#6428. Study of nearly 200,000 adults shows that eating snacks after dinner greatly increases the risk of liver disease

A study of nearly 200,000 adults links late-night eating to a much higher rate of liver disease, though direct causation remains unproven.

People who snacked after dinner or after going to bed had a 20 to 30 percent higher rate of liver disease than those who did not, according to researchers at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). The finding comes from nearly 200,000 U.S. adults followed in three long-running health studies.

The conditions included fatty liver disease and cirrhosis, a serious form of liver scarring.

The research is observational and relied on habits that participants reported themselves. A follow-up study at the same university will now test whether eating earlier helps.

Earlier research had already tied late-night snacking to heart disease and obesity, the OHSU team noted. The researchers set out to see whether the same habit was also tied to liver problems.

Robert Wilechansky, M.D., a hepatologist at OHSU who specializes in liver transplantation, is the study’s lead author.

Night shift workers, whose day-night cycle is out of step, have higher rates of both conditions. That pattern led Wilechansky to wonder whether small changes in meal timing could make a difference.

“A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease,” Wilechansky said.

His co-authors include Kevin Casey, Andrew Chan and Tracey Simon of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. OHSU announced the results on October 9, 2026.

The team analyzed three large, preexisting nationwide datasets. Two came from the Nurses’ Health Study, established in 1976, and the Nurses’ Health Study II.

Across three generations, the nurses’ studies count more than 280,000 participants.

The third source was the Health Professionals Follow-up Study. Launched in 1986, it enrolled 51,529 men working as dentists, pharmacists, optometrists, veterinarians and in other health professions.

Those men answer health questionnaires every two years and detailed diet questionnaires every four years.

Participants self-reported their diet and lifestyle habits, including whether they ate late. The team defined late-night eating as eating after dinner or after bedtime.

People were grouped by eating behavior. The researchers then looked for correlations with reported cases of MASLD or cirrhosis.

The first condition was metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD.

In MASLD, excess fat builds up in the liver for reasons other than heavy drinking, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).

The institute estimates that about 24 percent of U.S. adults have MASLD. OHSU puts the share of Americans affected at as much as 30 percent.

Overweight or obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and abnormal blood fats all raise the risk, the NIDDK lists.

In a more severe form, fat comes with inflammation and damage. That form may lead to cirrhosis, the second condition examined, in which the liver is scarred and permanently damaged.

Cirrhosis can in turn lead to liver cancer. Yet MASLD is usually silent, and even cirrhosis can develop with no symptoms.

“We know the liver is very much in tune with the body’s circadian rhythms,” Wilechansky explained. “So we’re interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health, without changing the composition of what people eat.”

Andrew McHill, Ph.D., an associate professor and sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU, is a co-author.

“We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it’s sleep, eating or exercise, really matters,” McHill said.

“For example, we have shown that eating during the night, when the internal biological clock is promoting sleep, reduces the ability of your body to metabolize foods as efficiently and can eventually lead to obesity, diabetes and now poor liver health,” he continued.

The analysis does not prove that late eating damages the liver. It shows an association between eating times and later diagnoses.

Wilechansky cautions that the findings come from observational, broadly defined, self-reported data.

The authors place their results within wider research on late eating and metabolic health.

Wilechansky is part of an OHSU team now recruiting for a new study. It will monitor eating behaviors directly and test whether eating earlier improves clinical measures of underlying MASLD.

“It’s important to remember, of the people who developed fatty liver disease, only a small fraction develop serious forms of the condition like liver cirrhosis,” Wilechansky noted.

“Even so, the big take-away here is that confining your calorie intake to several hours before bedtime might be beneficial,” he added.

The study was published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

A Roman-era belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest hints at the ancient conflict between the Romans and the Dacians.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. #6426. Van Gogh’s Starry Night shows a real night sky, study suggests

For decades, art historians and astronomers have wondered whether the sky of Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night shows real stars or imagined ones. A new study argues the stars are real — and that Van Gogh likely saw them a month later than most scholars thought.

The study, published Oct. 22 in Scientific Reports, comes from a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of the South Korean telescope maker SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University’s School of Space Research in Yongin.

By combining astronomical data, historical primary sources, and statistical analysis, the team narrowed the celestial alignments shown in the painting’s sky to a handful of late-July mornings.

They further suggest Van Gogh likely painted the eastern sky as seen from his asylum room in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, around 3 a.m. on July 22, 1889. That morning, a waning crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades — the V-shaped star cluster in Taurus the Bull — were all gathered in the same small patch of sky.

RELATED: Exploring the solar system through space art

In May 1889, Van Gogh admitted himself to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, a former monastery outside Saint-Rémy. The previous December, after a falling-out with fellow painter Paul Gauguin, he had cut off his left ear, and more breakdowns followed. At the asylum he kept working, producing some 150 paintings, including famous works like Almond Blossom and The Starry Night.

On June 18, he wrote to his brother Theo that he had begun “a new study of a starry sky.” For most scholars, that line anchored the painting to the mid-June sky.

In 1984, art historian Albert Boime argued the painting likely shows the dawn of June 19, with the constellation Aries at its center. Two years later, astronomer Charles Whitney used weather records to rule out the 19th and suggested the sky was actually a composite. With the two theories at odds, the idea that Van Gogh painted real stars faded to what the authors call a “marginal minority view.” Most scholars granted only that the bright point near the horizon was likely Venus.

Kim’s team thought the stars were most likely real, and that the early studies were incomplete. No one had tested the painter’s field of view, the shape of its pattern of stars, and the historical record together. Plus, on the morning of June 19, the Moon was a waning gibbous, past half and nothing like the slim crescent depicted on the canvas.

Rather than assuming a date, the researchers asked whether the sky Van Gogh painted could occur, and when. Their method has two core steps. First, they compare a painted sky with astronomical simulations to see whether its arrangement is even possible. Then, they use a statistical method that measures the similarity between two shapes — called Procrustes analysis — to see how faithfully the painting’s star patterns matched real ones. When more historical data is available, the team also works to reconstruct the artist’s field of view from the landscape and check candidate dates against weather records and letters.

As a proof of concept, they applied the method to a handful of other night paintings. A 2011 study had argued that the stars in German painter Adam Elsheimer’s 1609 The Flight into Egypt weren’t copied from a single real sky, and the team’s test agreed. The painting’s Big Dipper sits at an angle to the Milky Way that never occurs in the night sky.

French painter Jean-François Millet’s Starry Night, painted between 1850 and 1865, has no letters, weather records, or known painting site to draw on, so the team ran only the core astronomical tests. The painting’s depiction of Orion — including the bright star Rigel — and Sirius revealed the tightest fit of any painting in the study to an actual star pattern.

Van Gogh’s own 1888 Starry Night Over the Rhône and Café Terrace at Night were next. Because their painting sites in Arles still stand and his letters and local weather records survive, they got the full treatment. The Big Dipper in Starry Night Over the Rhône matched the real sky with what the authors call “relative precision,” and the Summer Triangle in Café Terrace at Night fit even more closely.

RELATED: How Galileo blended science and art before his death 380 years ago

Then came The Starry Night. Van Gogh is thought to have based the painting’s village on an earlier sketch he had completed of Saint-Rémy. After locating a ridge near the asylum whose view matches the drawing, the team found the sketch captures a zoomed-in slice of the landscape. Measured diagonally, from one corner of the frame to the opposite corner, the field of view spans about 18°. They then made an assumption: that Van Gogh likely framed the painting’s night sky the same way. If he did, there should be a morning on record when the Moon, Venus, and a recognizable star pattern all fit inside that narrow frame and are arranged as painted.

Only three dawns in June and July 1889 put the Moon above Venus, as in the painting, inside that field of view: June 23, July 22, and July 23. Only the July mornings also placed the Hyades in view, and on July 22, the Moon and Venus sat in opposite corners with the cluster in between.

At the center of the canvas, a cluster of stars forms a lopsided V that closely resembles the shape of the Hyades cluster. But any handful of dots can coincidentally look like a V. The team had to evaluate whether these stars were intentionally painted as the Hyades or just happened to resemble the cluster’s shape.

They reasoned that if Van Gogh had painted the real cluster, each painted star should have a real counterpart in the same spot. That is, the star at the point of the painted V should match the star at the point of the real V, and so on down each arm of the cluster. Matching them up that way should give a better fit than any other possible combination. So the team tried every possible way of pairing the five painted stars with the five real ones — 120 combinations in all — and measured how well each fit. The natural, point-to-point pairing was the most accurate.

The match was close, but it wasn’t perfect. Of all the paintings the team tested, The Starry Night fit its stars with the lowest statistical accuracy. The authors also acknowledge that a close shape match alone can’t identify a star group. Some other constellations score as well or better and are ruled out only by other evidence, such as where they sat in the sky that morning. Nevertheless, the combined evidence still suggested July 22 as the most likely date.

One objection to this scenario remained. Historians have long held that a severe seizure in mid-July left Van Gogh unable to work. But after rereading his letters alongside weather records from that summer, the team argues the seizure may have struck later, in the last week of July, leaving Van Gogh free to watch the dawn sky on July 22.

The authors argue that the fact that so many clues converge on one morning makes it “hard to reconcile with the premise that the sky on the canvas is an arbitrary creation.” The simpler explanation is that the painting’s sky is rooted in actual observations of the sky on that morning in July — and the burden of proof now falls on anyone who says Van Gogh invented it.

Because the core test needs nothing but the star positions, the team argues it could be turned on other night paintings, including many no one has yet examined. “I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-Rémy paintings, and at Van Gogh’s movements that summer,” Kim said in a statement. “Our conversation with Van Gogh’s other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one.”

Stellarium, the free planetarium software the team used to cross-check its simulations, lets you simulate the night sky from any place and date. Enter Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, and set the clock to a couple hours before sunrise on July 22, 1889. If the sky looks too bright, turn off the atmosphere in the view settings (or press the keyboard shortcut, A).

Then search for the Hyades cluster. Brilliant Venus sits on one side, a slim crescent Moon slightly higher on the other, and between them the V of the Hyades. You can scroll through the hours to watch the scene wheel up from the horizon before dawn. Then step back a day to July 21, or ahead to July 23 and 24, and watch the Moon slide toward Venus. Or compare the view with June 19, the date Boime proposed, and judge for yourself which sky best fits the canvas.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6425. A 4,000-year-old wall was found hiding underneath a Moroccan ridge that a French archaeologist sketched in the 1930s

Charcoal beneath a wall Armand Ruhlmann recorded in 1936 at Oued Beht, Morocco, dates its first phase to as early as 2010 BC.

In 1936, the French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann published photographs and a sketch of the walls on a ridge at Oued Beht, in Morocco’s Khémisset Province. He took them for a prehistoric enclosure. Under the stones he described, a wall dated about 4,000 years old remained buried.

It turned up in a trench dug by hand across the largest wall during the 2023 field season, which ran from October 30 to November 17. Charcoal from its cobble foundation gave a radiocarbon range of 2010 to 1747 BC.

The trench belongs to the Oued Beht Archaeological Project, with partners in Rabat, Rome and Cambridge. Its results are now out in Libyan Studies.

The paper reports a ditch, an earth bank and a wall from the early to mid-second millennium BC, and it leaves their purpose open.

Four stone alignments run east to west over the southern end of the ridge, above a river that flows all year. The village of Aït Siberne shows to the east in drone photographs taken by Toby Wilkinson of Cambridge.

Ruhlmann tied the biggest alignment, now labeled Wall B1, to a slighter wall on the western scarp and to Wall C further south. He read them as an éperon barré, or barred spur. That is a headland closed off on its open side by a rampart.

Giulio Lucarini of Italy’s National Research Council and Cyprian Broodbank of Cambridge are the corresponding authors of the new paper. They and 19 co-authors call Ruhlmann’s plan a “neat but unproven reconstruction.”

A French and Moroccan project dug into Wall B1 and Wall C between 2013 and 2015. That work is unpublished, and the remnants of its trenches were still open in 2022 and 2023.

Local residents told the team that the upper stonework had been bigger within living memory. The wall had also been turned into a stable for animals.

Trench 3 was laid out as a long slit across Wall B1. Its northern extension, Trench 3.1, was offset to keep clear of an olive tree. Work there stopped at about 4 feet (1.2 meters) for safety.

The visible wall, numbered F.300.2, is about 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) wide at ground level and 4.4 feet (1.35 meters) high. It is built of limestone blocks and cobbles in compacted earth.

Under it lay F.300.1, an older structure of burnt and unburnt daub, a building mud, with ashy lenses full of charcoal. It sat on rounded river or beach cobbles less than 4 inches (10 centimeters) across. All 17 sherds from it were prehistoric.

A second charcoal date, from the burnt material, gave 1896 to 1623 BC. The authors link that layer to the destruction of the first wall.

The team had expected Wall B1 to widen the site’s time range. “This expectation was spectacularly fulfilled,” the authors wrote.

North of the wall, Trench 3.1 ran into a ditch parallel to it. It was about 6 feet (1.84 meters) wide and at least 2 feet (65 centimeters) deep, and its base may not have been reached. One of its fills held a polished stone axe, and all 18 sherds from the ditch were prehistoric.

Bulk soil samples of 10 to 20 liters (about 3 to 5 gallons) went through flotation, which lifts seeds and charcoal off in water. Three charred seeds of domesticated crops from the ditch came back at about 1500 to 1300 BC.

The lowest phase of the earth bank gave 1532 to 1424 BC and 1497 to 1300 BC. A slanted posthole north of the wall, probably for a timber prop, held a legume seed dated to 1502 to 1324 BC.

Altogether the two trenches produced 17 dates, eight on seeds and nine on charcoal. Two charcoal samples with modern results were treated as intrusive and set aside.

The wall line follows the contact between Jurassic dolostone on the south and the Blue Marl Formation on the north. In their conclusions, the authors call the Wall B1 sequence “the earliest such constructions confirmed in the region.” Defense is one reading, but other motives for enclosure “cannot be excluded at this stage,” they wrote.

An earlier paper in Antiquity dated a farming community on the northern ridge to about 3400 to 2900 BC. Its authors called it currently the earliest and largest agricultural complex in Africa beyond the Nile corridor.

After the 2023 survey, that settlement is put at 10 to 11 hectares (25 to 27 acres). It has yielded bell-shaped storage pits, painted pottery and polished stone axes. Plant remains include barley, durum wheat, pea and wild olive.

In the second millennium BC, the activity moved south to the narrow tip. Morocco is better known for far older material, such as shell beads 142,000 to 150,000 years old and hominin jawbones from Casablanca.

The paper sets Oued Beht next to Kach Kouch, a site near the Mediterranean coast. People lived there late in the second millennium BC.

The authors suggest the two may mark a Bronze Age in northwestern Morocco, in step with the Argaric culture, a Bronze Age society in southern Spain. In those centuries, a fire at Cabezo Redondo in Spain preserved a wooden loom.

Medieval builders went back to the same line. Charcoal from the middle phase of the bank gave two dates in the 11th to 12th centuries AD. A stone wall just north of Wall B1 gave the 11th to 13th.

The standing stone wall belongs to that later phase, according to the paper, because the upper layers of the bank probably went up at about the same time. A seed from the fill inside the wall gave 1729 to 1516 BC, which the authors put down to older soil reused as fill.

At the northern edge of the site, local people had reported human remains in 2022, during house building. The team dug three test trenches there. Trench 7 exposed a burial with its skull to the west, and a molar dated it to the 13th century AD.

Across a shallow valley, about 1,640 feet (500 meters) away, survey walkers found a dense spread of 11th to 13th century pottery on a hilltop. One sherd, painted cobalt blue, was likely made in Fez.

Wall C, the southern piece of Ruhlmann’s plan, has no dates. Whether the three walls ever formed one enclosure is still unknown.

A copper-based rod 2.2 inches (5.5 centimeters) long came from the bank south of Wall B1. Its layer has no radiocarbon date, and no Bronze Age metal has been confirmed at Oued Beht so far.

Each radiocarbon date gives the earliest possible age of its layer. Charcoal and seeds can predate the soil that buried them.

Ruhlmann’s 1936 sketch showed Wall B1 as a rampart of unknown age. Its first phase now has two charcoal dates, and the authors have proposed limited work on Wall C.

The project runs under a memorandum of understanding between Morocco’s National Institute of Archaeological Sciences and Heritage, the National Research Council of Italy, ISMEO (the International Association for Mediterranean and Oriental Studies) and Cambridge’s McDonald Institute. The paper thanks the Oukhayi family for letting the team dig on their property.

The full study was published in the journal Libyan Studies.

#6424. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.
