#6420. Researchers hung baited cameras off a boat and identified 50 different oceanic whitetip sharks using only their fins

Baited cameras off Cat Island, The Bahamas, filmed 50 oceanic whitetip sharks that researchers told apart by dorsal fin markings over two seasons.

In late April 2023, a Florida International University (FIU) crew off Cat Island in The Bahamas started dropping baited GoPro cameras over the side. The goal was to film oceanic whitetip sharks about 43 feet (13 meters) down, with 2 pounds (1 kilogram) of bonito as bait.

They came back in 2024 and did it again. By then the video showed 50 separate whitetips. Each one was picked out by the notches, shape and pigmentation pattern of its first dorsal fin, the tall fin on the back.

Candace Fields, who is Bahamian and got her PhD in marine biology at FIU in 2025, ran the survey. Counting fins sometimes put up to three times as many sharks at a camera as the usual tally. All of it, though, comes from one island and two springs of fieldwork.

According to NOAA Fisheries, oceanic whitetips can reach 11 feet (3.4 meters). They spend most of their time in the top 656 feet (200 meters) of the open ocean.

NOAA puts the drop across the Pacific at about 80 to 95 percent since the mid-1990s. It names bycatch in commercial fisheries and demand for the fins as the main threat, and says some recent recovery is possible in the Pacific.

A Mote Marine Laboratory report found that most species in the shark fin trade are threatened with extinction. The IUCN lists the oceanic whitetip as Critically Endangered, and the U.S. Endangered Species Act lists it as threatened.

Yannis Papastamatiou is an FIU marine biologist at the university’s Institute of Environment and one of Fields’ advisers. “When you’re talking about marine predators in the ocean, that’s very difficult to answer, much harder than with terrestrial predators,” he told FIU News.

“If you want an idea of the abundance of lions, you can do airplane surveys and count them. But in the marine environment, you can’t see things, so that’s very difficult to do.”

FIU researchers had already surveyed another shark species for 10 years at an atoll with baited cameras, FIU News reported. Off Cat Island the water was too deep to anchor cameras to the bottom.

Fields tried two kinds of rig in late April and early May of 2023 and 2024. One was a frame of 3/4-inch galvanized steel pipe holding at least two GoPro Hero9 Black cameras. It drifted on a rope under a float and a flagged marker buoy, with a dive weight underneath.

The other was a wire bait cage with a camera. It hung about 49 feet (15 meters) from a 79-foot (24-meter) Viking sportfishing yacht. In the acknowledgments, the authors thank Captain Scott Genereux for running the Lady G.

The crew put out 99 sets between Columbus Point and Tartar Bank, a shallow seamount west of the island. Of those, 76 hung from the boat and 23 drifted, each at least half a mile (800 meters) from the last. Whitetips came to 51 of them.

Some earlier accounts said whitetips home in on boat engines. In this survey the tethered cage drew no more sharks than the drifting rig. Whether the engine was on or off did not matter either.

More sharks turned up at Columbus Point, a shelf edge where tuna, wahoo and billfish feed in winter and spring. Windy days brought more of them too. The authors think the rigs drifted farther and the scent of bonito spread wider.

Fields told FIU News that reading whitetip fins is similar to reading the spots on a whale shark. In the Western Indian Ocean, photos of those spots helped track individual whale sharks over ten years.

Until now, whitetip photo ID came from divers, who could swim into position for a clean shot. “In a video survey, obviously, you have no means to control how the shark approaches the camera. So, one big question was: is this even viable?” Fields said.

Each time a whitetip came into view, an annotator saved a still of its first dorsal fin. A shark got its own code, such as OWT1, only once both sides of the fin were on camera.

Some sharks circled the rig again and again. Others swam in at angles that hid the markings, and glare and murky water hid more. Still, the team picked out at least one shark by its fin on 41 of the 51 sets with whitetips.

Twenty-five of the 50 sharks got full codes. The other 25 were told apart from the right side of the fin alone.

Twelve sharks were filmed on two or more sets in the same season. Two of them, OWT8 and OWT15, were first filmed in 2023 and came back to the cameras in 2024.

Most camera studies report MaxN, the largest number of one species seen in a single frame. The fin count and MaxN agreed on about 87 percent of sets. Most of those had no whitetip or just one.

With two whitetips on screen at once, the counts matched only 31 percent of the time. With three, it was 28 percent. Papastamatiou said fin IDs let a researcher review the footage and say “actually, that was three different sharks.”

Fields now works at the Cape Eleuthera Institute in Rock Sound, Eleuthera. “I think what FIU did for me was solidify the importance of coming back home to work. The Bahamas is a big hub for shark research, and there are little to no Bahamians involved in that work,” she told FIU News.

Her other adviser, Demian Chapman, now works at Mote Marine Laboratory in Sarasota, Florida. Fields said both men pushed her to stick with it and become a Bahamian shark expert.

The 99 sets are a first count for whitetips in The Bahamas. They say nothing yet about whether the population is rising or falling.

On some sets no fin could be read. In those cases the team used MaxN. On three sets it told sharks apart by sex, a tag or fishing gear hanging from the body. The data are not in a public archive, and the paper says Fields will share them on reasonable request.

The authors also note that The Bahamas is a shark sanctuary but whitetips swim out of it into fished waters. In the Marshall Islands, scientists found that a shark sanctuary offered little protection from illegal fishing.

Next, the team wants cameras at more points along the archipelago, to see whether the sharks stay put or travel between islands. Fields also hopes to add photos from citizen scientists to the fin catalog.

OWT8 and OWT15 first swam up to the bonito off Cat Island in the spring of 2023. A year later both were back.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Biology.

#6419. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 5: Smoke out the Southern Cigar

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Tonight’s target is a bit of a test: How far south can you see? At a latitude of 40° north, NGC 55 in Sculptor — also called the Southern Cigar Galaxy or the String of Pearls Galaxy — only rises about 10° above the southern horizon at its highest, which occurs around 9 P.M. local time. Observers farther south will see it higher in the sky, while those farther north will see it closer to the horizon or be unable to make it out at all.

For those observers who can catch it, NGC 55 is a bright, 8th-magnitude edge-on barred spiral located just under 4° northwest of magnitude 2.4 Alpha (α) Phoenicis in Phoenix, which sits below the galaxy as you look south around this time of night. This galaxy is not only bright, it’s quite large, stretching roughly the width of the Full Moon (½°) at its longest. It is quite thin, however, only some 6’ wide along the other dimension. You’ll immediately see that its nucleus is not in the center, but offset to the west. Several other bright knots of star formation may also be visible within the galaxy’s plane — particularly if you drop in a nebula filter.

#6418. Foreign visitors to medieval Rome had to change their money, but the Anglo-Saxons kept their coins

Twenty Anglo-Saxon coins dug up beside the Vatican point to a busy English quarter in Rome where English money may have changed hands freely.

An Anglo-Saxon traveler heading for Rome in the ninth century had to think about money before leaving. The city ran on the pope’s coins, and foreign ones were not supposed to be accepted there.

Twenty silver coins from England have now come out of the ground near the Vatican, most of them from rubbish pits. English pilgrims and settlers lost them, one by one, over decades, in the quarter where they lived.

The archaeologists found these Anglo-Saxon coins mixed in with papal and Roman coins, among workshops. The two historians who studied them say the English may have been allowed to spend their own money in Rome.

The finds are also the first physical trace of the English quarter that medieval texts describe.

Rory Naismith studies early medieval England in the Department of Anglo-Saxon, Norse and Celtic at the University of Cambridge. Francesca Tinti is a medieval historian at the University of the Basque Country.

In an interview with Earth.com, Naismith said the two had wondered for years what a dig at one particular church would turn up. Santo Spirito in Sassia sits in the middle of the old English quarter.

“Our hope was that it might produce artifacts and coins from England in the early Middle Ages,” he said.

“The Palazzo della Rovere site is literally across the road from the church, so the surprise (in a way) was that our imagined discoveries turned out to be what was actually found.”

Archaeologists began digging under the walled garden of the Palazzo della Rovere in 2020, while the building was being turned into a hotel. In 2023, the same dig found the remains of the emperor Nero’s theater.

Rome’s state archaeology office, the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma, directed the excavation, and a team coordinated by Marzia Di Mento did the fieldwork.

Thirty coins came out of the ground, and 23 of them were struck in the tenth century. Twenty were Anglo-Saxon: 19 silver pennies and one halfpenny.

They carry the names of Alfred the Great’s son, Edward the Elder, and his grandsons Æthelstan and Eadred, who ruled between 899 and 955.

Fourteen Anglo-Saxon coins had fused into two lumps of six and eight after a thousand years underground. The pennies Naismith and Tinti could read closely came from East Anglia, Kent, London and the West Midlands.

Alongside them lay a coin probably struck for Pope John X, two from the mint at Pavia in northern Italy, and a handful of Roman bronzes. Around the coins was the debris of leather, bone and metalwork production, spread over at least 32,000 square feet (3,000 square meters).

The coins were not one buried hoard. They lay scattered across five spots, with the two biggest groups in rubbish pits. Each of those groups held Anglo-Saxon, Italian and Roman coins together.

Naismith and Tinti considered whether the silver was being collected to melt down, and found nothing on the site to suggest it. There wasn’t a trace of silver working at all.

The halfpenny pointed the same way, because small change like that turns up rarely in hoards and often where lots of low-value trading went on.

Naismith told Earth.com that each coin was worth tens of modern dollars and was relatively rare in the tenth century.

“People would not have lost them lightly,” he said. “So, to find this many in one place suggests these coins were being used intensively, for lots of transactions. In other words, this was a vibrant area.”

Written records from Rome in this period mention only papal money, and the historians read that as the rule.

Foreign coin was not normally acceptable, and one ninth-century letter mentions a Frankish abbot who worried about changing his currency before a trip to the city.

English silver pennies have turned up in Rome before. One in a hoard from the House of the Vestals in the Forum, and another near the Vatican Radio station.

Until now, though, none had come from the heart of the English quarter itself, the Schola Saxonum, which texts place in this area from the late eighth century.

“The coins aren’t pretty but they have a lot to say,” Naismith said.

“More Anglo-Saxon coins from this period have now been found in Rome than papal coins. This sounds bizarre, but it’s telling us that a very large amount of money was flowing in from England at this time.”

The dates give the historians a clue. The Rome finds cluster between about 900 and 970. That is before the English began the annual payment to the pope known as Peter’s Pence, so the coins are unlikely to be pious offerings.

What was happening instead, Naismith and Tinti suggest, is a deal. Alfred the Great sent alms to Rome in 883 and again in the late 880s.

At Alfred’s request, Pope Marinus I freed the English quarter “from every tribute and toll,” according to Asser, the Welsh scholar who wrote Alfred’s biography in 893.

No surviving source spells out what that privilege covered. The pair propose that the right to spend English money was part of it.

The use of English coin in Rome faded around the 970s, and the historians aren’t sure why.

One possibility they raise is that the popes stopped minting their own coins at about that time. The privilege may have depended on the popes actively running the local money system.

The findings appear as a chapter, written in Italian, in the proceedings of a conference held at Roma Tre University in December 2025. The full catalog of the coins is still to come.

Nobody knows how large the English quarter was, or whether Alfred himself secured the currency arrangement. Asser’s line is the only written hint, and the historians call it a possibility rather than a proof.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Naismith said more digging on neighboring sites would be ideal. In a city like Rome, he said, the chance only comes when building or utility work opens the ground, as the hotel project did here.

“The church of S. Spirito in Sassia would be especially interesting to look into further,” he said. Until that ground opens, the coins and craft debris from one garden are the only physical trace of the English quarter anyone has seen.

The full study has not been published in a journal. It appears as a chapter in the book of conference proceedings titled Rome and the Others (300-1000), published by SAP Società Archeologica (ISBN: 9791256820405).

#6416. Nov. 5, 2006: Mars Global Surveyor goes quiet

Designed to study Mars in a comprehensive way, examining its atmosphere, its interior, and its surface, the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) launched Nov. 7, 1996. By Sept. 12, 1997, it would reach Mars and slip into orbit around the Red Planet. Over the next nine years, it revealed an evolving world of ongoing geological dynamism, analyzed the history of water on Mars, tracked the movements of ice at its poles, and analyzed its topography and weather. With nearly 200,000 photos captured, MGS supplied more images of Mars than all the missions before it – combined. It also helped NASA plan for future rover missions to the Red Planet.

MGS substantially exceeded its two-year mission, but on Nov. 2, 2006, the orbiter signaled to NASA that it was experiencing difficulties with its solar panels. Two days without communication followed. On Nov. 5, more signals were sent, and then MGS went silent. The mission officially ended on Nov. 14, with NASA concluding a battery failure had caused a computer error that closed out MGS’s tour.

#6415. Two decades of tracking data on Manx shearwaters shows the seabirds actually get jet lag just like humans do

GPS tracks of 1,045 Manx shearwaters over 20 years show fast eastward flights leave their body clocks up to an hour behind, bending their sun compass.

Manx shearwaters from Skomer Island, off the Pembrokeshire coast of Wales, sometimes fly about 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) west into the Atlantic to feed. On the flight back east, some go fast enough to get a kind of jet lag.

The sun comes up earlier the farther east a bird is. After a long day flying east, a shearwater’s body clock can run up to an hour behind.

Oxford biologists saw the effect in the birds’ tracks. The steering errors went up to about 15 degrees. The team does not yet know if the lag does the birds any other harm.

Lewin and 23 co-authors published the paper in Science on October 29, 2026. It used 20 years of GPS data from 1,045 Manx shearwaters on 3,688 foraging trips.

Professor Tim Guilford, a co-author, belongs to the Oxford Navigation Group, which works mostly on Skomer and on Lighthouse Island in County Down.

The group’s GPS loggers were first designed for geotagging photos on backpacking trips, its project page says. Team members take them apart and wrap them in heat-shrink plastic.

The birds came from seven colonies. The R code the team put on Zenodo lists Skomer, Skokholm, Ramsey, Lundy, Copeland, Rum and St Kilda. Skomer has nearly 350,000 breeding pairs, the Wildlife Trust of South and West Wales says.

In the code, every track was cut down to one GPS fix every five minutes. A trip home only counted if it started at least 31 miles (50 kilometers) out. It also had to end at least 25 percent closer.

Birds that use the sun as a compass also need to know the time. The sun moves across the sky all day. Normally they set their body clock at sunrise, the University of Oxford said.

A drawing released with the paper shows how this goes wrong. In it, a shearwater starts for home at 30 degrees west. Its clock matches local time there.

Six hours later the bird is at 15 degrees west, where the sun came up an hour sooner. The sun now sits about 20 degrees clockwise of where the bird expects it. So the bird turns about 20 degrees clockwise of its proper heading.

Birds in the GPS records drifted clockwise as they flew east. Dr. Patrick Lewin of Oxford’s Department of Biology, who led the work, said that is the pattern a clock running late would produce.

For each fix, the code works out where the sun would be from the spot where the bird saw sunrise that day. Crosswind and distance from the colony go into the models as well.

Magnetic values for every fix came from the International Geomagnetic Reference Field, via a program called geomag70. The sun model beat the magnetic one.

In Japan, streaked shearwaters were used to study how birds rely on an inner compass tied to magnetic sensing.

Lewin said it is “amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction.”

The code also checks whether a straight line from each fix to the colony crosses land.

A comment in the code says the team had to leave out points around St. David’s Head for Skomer and Skokholm. Without that step, every point to the north would count as having no clear line home because of a small stretch of land.

Along coasts the birds kept making the same errors, flying nearer the shore when the predicted error pointed toward land and farther out when it pointed out to sea.

Guilford, a co-author, said the thinking of wild animals is hard to study. Measuring their natural movements carefully, he said, “can reveal the underlying behavioral mechanisms.”

The team worked out one case for an adult bird. It started 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) out with an average error of 7 degrees. It corrected its course all the way.

That bird would fly only about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) extra before getting within 3.1 miles of its colony.

A young bird on its first migration may not correct like that, Lewin’s group said. Its errors could add up to hundreds of kilometers. Caspian terns do not fly that first trip alone, because fathers lead young birds on their first migration.

Manx shearwaters spend the northern winter off Argentina, according to the Oxford group. Another Oxford-led study reported that the endangered Balearic shearwater changed its migration range mostly through individual flexibility.

People who fly fast across time zones get disturbed sleep and fatigue, according to the Oxford statement, and jet lag can also unsettle the gut and other organs.

The statement says more research is needed on whether wild birds suffer any effects on health, behavior or survival. The hundreds of kilometers for young birds came from a calculation.

Lewin wants to find out what the lag does to them. “Do they mistime critical behaviors? Do they experience physiological side effects like we do?” he said in the University of Oxford statement.

Lewin also said the shearwaters, which make long flights all the time, might one day help people deal with jet lag. For now, they keep racing an earlier sunrise back to Skomer.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6414. Meteorites that may have delivered carbon to early Earth carry an oxygen signature older than their asteroids

Organic specks in primitive meteorites carry an oxygen signature set before their asteroids formed, likely in the cold outer solar system.

Some of the carbon on the early Earth may have arrived inside meteorites, carried as dark specks of organic matter far too small to see.

Where those specks were first made is still an open question. A new study suggests their oxygen dates from before the asteroids that carried them had formed.

In seven primitive meteorites that were never strongly heated, the organic matter carries nearly the same oxygen fingerprint.

Water on the asteroids barely changed it. That makes the oxygen a record of where the material formed, not of what happened to it later.

Where the organics formed is the team’s interpretation, drawn from a small set of meteorites and two lab tests.

Daniel Crocker and David Johnston of Harvard’s Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences led the work. Their co-authors were Conel Alexander of the Carnegie Institution for Science and Mark Thiemens of the University of California, San Diego.

Oxygen atoms come in three stable forms: oxygen-16, oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. They differ only in weight. Scientists call these forms isotopes, and the mix of the three in a sample works like a fingerprint.

On Earth, almost any process that sorts oxygen by weight changes the share of oxygen-17 about half as much as the share of oxygen-18.

The oldest minerals in some carbon-rich meteorites break that rule. In them, the two heavier forms change by equal amounts.

That odd pattern is usually explained as a blend of two ancient pools of oxygen, one rich in oxygen-16 and one poor in it. Researchers drew a reference line for it in 1977 from minerals in the Allende meteorite, but what produced it is still debated.

The meteorites in the study belong to a group called carbonaceous chondrites. The most primitive ones hold up to 4 percent carbon by weight in their organic matter. Between 30 and 80 percent of that organic matter won’t dissolve in acids or solvents.

Alexander’s lab separated that material from the rock. Crocker then measured its oxygen with a method the Harvard group had recently developed.

Water had altered the seven primitive meteorites on their home asteroids, always below about 302°F (150°C). Their organic matter came out almost identical.

The oxygen-18 readings varied by only about 2 parts per thousand, and every sample was within the margin of error of the reference line.

“What surprised me was how similar the oxygen isotope compositions were across meteorites that experienced very different alteration histories after they formed,” Crocker told Earth.com.

These asteroids once held liquid water, and water can swap oxygen atoms with the material around it.

The team calculated what would happen if the organic matter had traded much of its oxygen with that water. Its oxygen-18 reading would be 27 to 58 parts per thousand above a standard.

The actual readings were 10 to 12. So the organic matter most likely swapped very little oxygen with the water. If it had, samples from several separate asteroids would have needed nearly identical conditions to end up with the same values.

The water still changed the material’s chemistry, and some oxygen-bearing parts of the molecules were lost. But it left the oxygen’s mix of weights mostly alone.

“That preservation gives us an opportunity to look past what happened to the organic matter on the asteroids and investigate the environment in which it originally formed,” Crocker said.

Organic matter from six meteorites heated on their asteroids, or by impacts, looked different. It held less of both heavy oxygen forms, and the readings formed a trend away from the unheated group.

To test whether heat alone could do that, the team warmed organic matter from the Mighei meteorite in a vacuum for an hour. One run reached 932°F (500°C) and the other 1,112°F (600°C).

The samples lost about 59 and 67 percent of their oxygen respectively, and what remained shifted along the same trend as the heated meteorites. Undo the heating, and they would move back toward the primitive group, which fits one shared starting fingerprint.

Water didn’t set the fingerprint, and heat changes it in a different direction. So the authors concluded the oxygen most likely went in when the organic matter itself formed, before it was gathered into any asteroid.

The organic matter holds less oxygen-16 than almost every mineral in these meteorites. In the early solar system, water was the main ingredient low in oxygen-16. So the authors think the organics took their oxygen from ancient water as they formed.

Extra heavy hydrogen and nitrogen in the organics already hinted at a cold place with strong radiation. The team favors a birthplace in the outer solar system, with the same well-mixed supply ending up in several asteroids.

“Rather than starting with the chemistry that occurred on the early Earth, we can ask what organic material Earth and other young planets inherited from the Solar System environment in which they formed,” Crocker and Johnston told Earth.com.

The researchers said they “cannot yet identify a single location or oxygen-bearing molecule as its source.” They also checked for lab effects, such as stray mineral grains and the chemicals used to free the organics. They concluded neither changed the readings in any meaningful way.

The unusual pattern in the ancient minerals, first spotted more than 50 years ago, still lacks a full explanation. “That doesn’t solve the mystery, but it provides a new constraint,” the two researchers added.

Next, the team sees the oxygen as a way to narrow down where, and under what conditions, the material formed. That could show how widely the raw ingredients for life’s chemistry were spread among the young planets.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6412. Curiosity captures a martian dawn

The morning Sun casts a hazy glow over Mars’ Mount Sharp, lighting up distant wind-carved rock formations known as yardangs. This scene is cropped from a six-image panorama captured by the Mastcam on NASA’s Curiosity rover at 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 11, 2026, the mission’s 4,982nd sol (martian day). Mount Sharp, formally Aeolis Mons, stands 3.4 miles (5.5 km) tall at the center of Mars’ 96-mile-wide (154 km) Gale Crater. Since 2014, Curiosity has climbed roughly 0.6 mile (1 km) up its stratified slopes, reading each new layer like a chapter of martian geology.

The mountain’s lowest, oldest layers likely formed from sediment deposited by lakes and streams that have long since vanished. This photo is the most detailed view to date of the much younger yardang layer. Of particular interest is the fact that the color and orientation of the yardangs don’t match the surrounding material. Scientists think these features could have been built up from volcanic ash that settled after a nearby eruption, and was then carved away by the wind. Curiosity should reach the yardangs’ base in 2027, where its instruments will help uncover how the layer formed.

#6411. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6409. The herring that fed medieval Europe never ran out, yet the fishery that caught them collapsed

Overfishing, a cooling climate, shifting dunes and serfdom ended a medieval herring fishery, and the lessons apply to Baltic herring today.

When a fishery dies, the obvious explanation is that people caught all the fish. For the fishery that was once Europe’s main source of salted herring, that isn’t what happened. The herring were still there when the catch collapsed in the late 1500s.

A new study finds it took overfishing, a colder climate and a changing society, all at once, to end it.

For nearly 300 years, herring caught in the Sound, the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden, was salted and shipped from the British Isles to northern Italy.

Around 1570, the catch fell apart within a few years. It took until the 1950s for catches there to reach the same size again.

A team of fisheries economists, ecologists and historians led by Kiel University and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) set out to find out why.

Their catch numbers are rebuilt from scattered old records, so they show a smoothed trend rather than a count for every year.

“None of these factors alone would have brought the fishery down. It is their interplay that explains the dynamics,” said Rudi Voss, the study’s first author and a fisheries economist in iDiv’s Biodiversity Economics group.

For most of the period, no continuous catch records exist. The team’s time series runs from 1200 to 1650. It was pieced together from customs records, toll books and accounts of the king’s right to buy herring first.

Where those records went silent, the researchers filled gaps using salt. Salt was the trade’s most important supply, so how much of it was available set a limit on how much herring could be preserved and sold.

Most modern records of a fish population cover a few decades. This one is long enough to follow plagues, wars and climate swings across centuries.

Each autumn, fishing fairs near the small towns of Skanör and Falsterbo became busy trading centers. Between 1524 and 1570, the fishery landed about 61,000 tons (55,000 metric tons) of herring a year on average.

The researchers paired the catch history with old herring prices from markets in England, Hamburg, Brabant and Utrecht. From the two together, they estimated the largest catch the herring could have sustained year after year.

During the boom, the catch ran above that limit. The herring population shrank to between 41 and 51 percent of the largest size the team estimated for it. It didn’t crash, though.

In an interview with Earth.com, Voss said the size of the catch stood out to him. “Looking back at our analysis, I was surprised by the huge amount of herring catch being realized by very simple means,” he said.

He added that effective rules would have been needed even then to keep the catch sustainable. A few did exist: trawl nets were banned in 1371, and there are signs that net mesh size was regulated in 1386.

A smaller stock likely made each fish more expensive to catch. Meanwhile, the Little Ice Age was setting in, and herring that spawn in autumn fare poorly after harsh winters, so the stock replaced itself more slowly.

The fishing towns had their own troubles. Shifting dunes destroyed their infrastructure in the 1570s, and fishermen left for a herring boom on the Swedish west coast.

In the early 1600s, nobles enforced serfdom on peasants, barring them from leaving their landlords’ fields each autumn to fish.

Buyers were also turning to the North Sea, where boats were seaworthy and the season lasted three times as long.

To weigh all of this, the team drew a map of nine factors, from climate and war to workforce and demand. They marked whether each one pushed the others up or down.

Across the fishery’s four phases, the map’s predictions matched the catch history. Colder weather alone couldn’t explain it.

For centuries, those pressures partly canceled one another out. In the early 1500s, they all pushed the same way, and the fishery boomed. By the middle of the 1500s, the pressures had turned, and all of them pulled the catch down.

The medieval fishery caught herring that spawn in autumn. Today the main fishery in the western Baltic targets a different group that spawns in spring. That stock is outside safe biological limits, and scientists have advised a catch of zero.

Overfishing drove that decline, the authors wrote, and warmer water now makes recovery harder, much as cooling weighed on the medieval stock.

“Today’s fisheries management in the EU is still not sufficiently able to deal with climate change impacts and increasing cumulative (socio-economic) pressures,” Voss told Earth.com.

He called for a faster move toward ecosystem-based management, which weighs everything around a fish population instead of one species alone, and said it must include social and economic factors.

“If we fail to do so, we might see a number of fisheries going to share the fate of this historic fishery,” he said.

The catch history is a best estimate, and its certainty varies. The 1200s are inferred from salt production and population, while the decline after the 1570s rests on sparse tax records.

The old herring prices couldn’t be adjusted for changes in the value of money, so the authors warn that their results should be treated with caution. Their map of nine factors shows which way each pressure pushed the catch, not how hard.

The analysis can’t say whether the dunes, the cold or the lost workers mattered most in the final years.

Voss put the lesson plainly. “I think that we need to acknowledge that sustainable fisheries can only succeed if we take social and economic conditions just as seriously as the health of the stock itself,” he said.

The western Baltic now faces the same question. A recent German commission on the future of Baltic Sea fisheries proposed improving infrastructure and diversifying the local economy alongside the zero catch.

Whether the spring herring recovers will show if that is enough.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sustainability.

#6407. Lost audio recordings of Louisiana Creole give us a rare chance to hear the past voices of early New Orleans

Recordings from 1935 reveal how Louisiana Creole speakers switched languages, capturing speech patterns that written accounts often missed.

To understand how Louisiana Creole sounded in the 1800s, scholars have had to rely on writing. But some writers changed what they heard.

One researcher wrote in 1933 that he had “purified the dialect” in his transcriptions.

Recordings made two years later, now analyzed for the first time, capture something that those written accounts often missed: people moving between Creole and French as they spoke.

Lorenzo Dow Turner, remembered as the first African American linguist, recorded those voices on 13 aluminum discs, way back in 1935.

Oliver Mayeux, a linguist at the University of Cambridge’s Faculty of Modern and Medieval Languages and Linguistics, tracked down the digitized recordings and worked out who was speaking.

The discs contain the earliest known recordings of spoken Louisiana Creole and Louisiana French. Both languages now have dwindling numbers of elderly native speakers.

“Turner’s lost recordings contain far more linguistic diversity than the texts we relied upon until now,” said Mayeux.

“This is the language of the levees and cane fields. The language that drifted out from French Quarter saloons along with early jazz music at the turn of the last century.”

Louisiana Creole shares almost all its words with Louisiana French, but the two languages use different grammar.

Creole developed on southern Louisiana plantations, where enslaved people, mostly from West Africa, came into contact with settlers who spoke regional varieties of French.

“Africans with little common language were forced onto plantations where French was the language of administration. Everybody is learning approximations of French and then approximations of approximations. Quite quickly, a new language is born,” said Mayeux.

By Turner’s arrival in July 1935, younger people and city residents were already moving toward English. Mayeux, who has family ties in Louisiana, knows that history through his own family.

“By the middle of the 20th century you see the end of intergenerational transmission. My grandfather wanted his children to speak English,” explained Mayeux.

“This was typical of many Louisianans who saw their future as American rather than Creole or Cajun,” he added.

Many children, therefore, grew up without learning the language their parents spoke.

Turner was known for studying Gullah, a creole language with English roots spoken by Black communities in Georgia and South Carolina.

He visited Louisiana to compare the two languages’ sounds, especially how speakers’ voices rose and fell.

“From casual observation I find that the intonation of Creole resembles very much that of Gullah,” Turner wrote to a funding body after the trip.

His recording machine weighed about 100 pounds (45 kilograms). He had to drive it to places with electricity, which limited where he could work.

“Turner relied on a network of Black doctors and intellectuals in New Orleans and out in the country. The physicians found him Creole-speaking interviewees and let him record in their offices,” said Mayeux.

“These were trusted spaces for the participants during the era of Jim Crow segregation and, crucially, were wired for electricity.”

In Lafayette and Opelousas, doctors Julius Blackburn Matthews and August C. Terrence hosted the sessions. One participant, Marie Raymond, said she had never known a doctor until she was 69.

A woman also helped Turner conduct many interviews. She seemed more comfortable speaking French than he did, and Mayeux thinks she was probably Turner’s wife, Geneva Calcier Townes Turner.

Turner never analyzed the Louisiana Creole recordings, and his applications for funding to continue the comparison were rejected. The Guggenheim Foundation turned down one application and awarded a fellowship to his former student Zora Neale Hurston instead.

Mayeux suspects Turner simply set the discs aside. Indiana University’s Archives of Traditional Music later digitized them, but their labels offered little information and sometimes got it wrong.

One clue came from a disc that a Turner biography described as two people singing. It actually contained solo piano music by Jessie Covington Dent, a New Orleans pianist and civil rights activist.

Dent’s family papers at the Amistad Research Center led Mayeux to Turner’s papers. An address book there named the doctors who had hosted him.

Another disc listed “Mme Emma Bronssard,” which Mayeux recognized as a misspelling of Broussard. The woman said she was 69, had been widowed for 20 years, and had raised 12 children of her own plus four orphans.

Census and death records matched those details to Emma Benoit, born Emma Broussard.

Her great-granddaughter, Valencia Pradier-Linton, later shared a magazine interview in which Benoit’s son said his mother “didn’t know how to talk English at all.”

Turner recorded three Creole speakers in New Orleans, where people shifted to English earlier than in the countryside. The city’s variety of Creole likely has no speakers left.

Mayeux identified two speakers: George Doyle, born in 1867, and Odelia Edmond, born in 1862. Doyle had worked as a police officer before the city segregated its police department.

Some of their speech matched the old texts closely. Doyle’s word for policemen, “lapolis,” came from the French “la police,” but the French word for “the” had become a permanent part of the noun.

Edmond used mo for “my” when she said “my mother.” French would use a feminine form of the word instead.

Other details challenged what scholars thought they knew. The speakers used rounded vowels, like those in the French words “peu” and “plus,” which researchers had treated as a later borrowing.

Edmond also moved between old and newer forms of the same word. While explaining that she was three days old when her mother died, she used a long form of “have” known mainly from 19th-century writing.

Just 15 seconds later, when talking about being nine days old, she used the short form. Hearing both from the same speaker suggested that New Orleans Creole was more varied than the written record made it seem.

Outside New Orleans, speakers often began interviews in Louisiana French, the more formal language. Others in the room then asked them to speak Creole.

Emma Benoit started with a polite French greeting. In Mayeux’s translation, a woman interrupted with “no no no! Creole!” and then “no no that’s French; that’s not Creole anymore.”

Benoit replied in Creole, “I forget that,” and said she would talk about her troubles. A few minutes later, she returned to French and received another reminder.

Anastasie Dumas switched languages too, answering in French when Turner addressed her in formal, European-sounding French. When his co-interviewer asked in somewhat stiff Creole how to make gumbo, Dumas returned to Creole.

Most participants could not read or write and did not own a radio. Speaking into a visiting professor’s recording machine would have been an unusual, formal experience.

The people in the room and the occasion helped shape how they spoke. Mayeux concluded that French signaled politeness and respectability, while Creole emerged in more relaxed moments of joking and storytelling.

For most speakers today, moving between the two languages no longer carries the same degree of social meaning.

Each recording lasts about two to five minutes, and static makes some speech hard to follow. The New Orleans speakers also came through one circle of doctors, educators, and musicians, so their voices cannot represent the whole city.

Mayeux describes his reconstruction as partial and interpretive, shaped by his position as a white researcher listening nearly a century later. He hopes others will offer their own readings.

He also cannot yet explain why the city recordings differ from the old texts. The language may have changed, writers may have removed variation, or both may have happened.

The next step is comparison with recordings that Turner’s former student Raleigh Morgan Jr. made in the 1950s. Researchers can study those voices alongside the 1935 discs and the Creole spoken today.

For some young learners, Creole offers a way to reconnect with their family history. Many are grandchildren of native speakers whose parents never learned the language, Mayeux said.

“Young people are learning Creole to connect with the richness of their heritage, helping them discover a distinct identity in an increasingly homogenized world,” said Mayeux.

The study is published in the journal Language Documentation and Description.

#6406. Most lithium comes from desert ponds or hard-rock mines, and a new lab method skips both

Engineers pulled lithium from salty water in the lab using a solvent that reacts to heat, a step toward reaching brines that evaporation ponds can’t use.

The lithium in a battery usually comes from one of two places: a hard-rock mine, or a desert pond where the sun bakes salty water for up to two years.

Columbia University engineers have now pulled lithium out of salty water in the lab with neither one. Their solvent takes up lithium at room temperature and lets it go when the temperature rises.

Ngai Yin Yip, an associate professor of Earth and Environmental Engineering at Columbia, did the work with four co-authors. It’s a proof of concept. The team mixed salty water in the lab to copy the chemistry of the Salton Sea, a geothermal region in California.

About 40% of lithium production starts as brine, salty water that collects in large reservoirs under deserts. Nearly all of that lithium comes out through solar evaporation. Mining companies pump the brine into sprawling ponds and wait for the water to evaporate.

Evaporation ponds need a lot of dry, flat land, so they work in places like Chile’s Atacama Desert and parts of Nevada. They also use large volumes of water in places that can barely spare it. Hard-rock mining, the other main source, comes with steep tradeoffs of its own.

“There’s no way solar evaporation alone can match future demand,” Yip said. “And there are promising lithium-rich brines, like those in California’s Salton Sea, where this method simply can’t be used at all.”

The Salton Sea region holds enough lithium, by one estimate, for more than 370 million electric vehicle batteries.

Lithium-bearing brine turns up elsewhere in the U.S. too. In Arkansas, a U.S. Geological Survey-led study estimated 5 million to 19 million tons of lithium in brine beneath the southwestern part of the state.

In Pennsylvania, analysts who studied company data on wastewater from 515 gas wells found lithium in it as well.

The solvent is a liquid chemical that behaves differently depending on temperature. At room temperature, it attracts water. When it warms, it repels water.

The team mixed the solvent with brine at room temperature, and the solvent took up water and lithium together. Then the team warmed it a little.

The solvent now repelled water, so it released the lithium and the water as a purified stream. It returned to its starting state, ready to reuse.

The warming step needs only modest heat. “It can be powered by low-grade heat from waste sources or solar collectors,” Yip said.

In brine, lithium mixes with sodium and potassium, two metals that behave a lot like it, and separating the three is hard. The solvent still preferred lithium to sodium across versions with different chemical structures, by as much as about 10 to 1.

The solvent kept that preference even when lithium was 1,000 times scarcer than sodium or potassium in the water. In the simulated Salton Sea brine, the preference reached about 13 to 1 over sodium and 24 to 1 over potassium. So the solvent still separated lithium when lithium made up only a tiny share of the metals in the water.

Magnesium, another common contaminant in lithium brines, also dropped out as a solid, because the solvent is alkaline, the opposite of acidic. In the Salton Sea mixture, the team removed all of it.

The team reused one batch of solvent for four rounds. Together, the four rounds recovered nearly 40% of the lithium in the simulated brine. The solvent kept its preference for lithium throughout.

So about 60% of the lithium went unrecovered after four rounds. The team hasn’t yet optimized the system for yield or efficiency, so 40% reflects an early version of the method.

The team ran its tests in the lab, in batches, on brines it mixed itself. Real brine from the ground may hold more impurities than the lab mixes did, and the team still has to show how the solvent handles them. The same goes for its performance at the size of a working plant.

Whether recovery rises above 40% once the team tunes the system remains an open question. Columbia has invited companies that want to collaborate on the technology, or license it, to express their interest.

The full study was published in the journal Joule.

#6405. Decades of clues helped scientists discover a massive freshwater lake miles beneath the ice in Antarctica

Lake Vostok, a vast freshwater lake hidden beneath 2.5 miles of Antarctic ice, was mapped using radar, seismic data and satellite measurements.

In June 1996, a paper in Nature described a large, deep freshwater lake beneath the ice of central East Antarctica. The lake, now called Lake Vostok, lies under about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) of ice.

The authors found that its area was about 50 percent larger than earlier estimates, with dimensions comparable to those of Lake Ontario.

The paper drew on clues that had been building for decades. They ranged from seismic soundings in the 1960s to airborne radar flights and, in 1993, satellite measurements.

The lake takes its name from Russia’s Vostok Station, which sits above its southern tip, according to Michael Studinger, then at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The former Soviet Union set up the station in 1957. It lies about 800 miles (1,300 kilometers) from the geographic South Pole, on roughly 2.3 miles (3,700 meters) of ice, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory.

About 30 people work at the station during the summer research season.

In 1983, the station’s air temperature fell to -129°F (-89°C).

Far below, the lake water sits under more than 360 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level.

Where the ice sheet crosses the lake, it goes afloat, Studinger writes. In some areas, lake water freezes onto the base of the ice.

Russian scientists suggested from seismic soundings in the 1960s that water might lie beneath the ice. Later, a joint U.S., British and Danish airborne radar project found flat reflections that pointed to water.

A 1974 to 1975 airborne radio-echo survey outlined a lake of about 3,900 square miles (10,000 square kilometers), the 1996 paper reports.

Robin Bell, a geophysicist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, described those flights in a NASA Earthdata feature.

“Scientists flew around Antarctica in C-130 airplanes that sent electromagnetic waves through the ice sheet,” Bell said.

The flat layers in the radar records were the first signs of subglacial lakes, or water trapped beneath the ice. At the time, researchers took them for small, isolated ponds.

“Quite frankly they didn’t seem to be important,” Bell recalled.

In the 1990s, the European Remote Sensing satellite, ERS-1, produced the first comprehensive map of Antarctica’s ice surface using radar altimetry, the same feature says.

Scientists studying that map noticed an unusually flat area near the center of the ice sheet, about the size of Lake Ontario.

“The ice surface will look rugged. But if water is underneath, the ice surface will look very flat,” Bell explained.

In 1993, satellite altimetry independently confirmed the extent of the lake first outlined by radar, the 1996 authors wrote.

The paper’s five authors came from Russian and British institutions. They included Andrey Kapitsa of Moscow State University and Martin Siegert, then at the University of Wales.

Another author was glaciologist Gordon de Quetteville Robin of the University of Cambridge’s Scott Polar Research Institute.

The team combined new altimetry and radio-echo data with existing seismic data. They found that the lake was deep, with an average depth of 410 feet (125 meters) or more, and that its water was fresh.

The team also estimated that water stays in the lake for tens of thousands of years. They put the mean age of the water at about one million years.

That age counts from when the water was deposited as surface ice on the ancient Antarctic ice sheet.

The regional flow of the ice could be explained as steady flow along and over the lake.

Robin had suggested in the 1950s that geothermal heat from the bedrock could warm the base of the ice sheet. He could not prove it until ice-penetrating radar arrived in the 1970s.

The base of the ice stays warm because of geothermal heating from Earth’s interior, Siegert wrote in a 2005 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences paper. About 50 milliwatts of heat per square meter is enough to melt the base of an ice sheet 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) thick.

The same review describes the lake as over 155 miles (250 kilometers) long, with depths reaching about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in places. It is one of over 100 subglacial lakes identified beneath Antarctica.

In 2012, a Russian team drilled all the way down to the lake to look for microbes, NASA’s Earth Observatory reported. Scientists estimate the lake has been sealed under ice for up to 25 million years.

Studinger also calls Lake Vostok the closest terrestrial analog to Europa, the ice-covered moon of Jupiter.

The study was published in the journal Nature.

A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

Adriani et al. (2026). Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NET/ORCA. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. https://doi.org/10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012

#6402. The mystery of long COVID: What lasting health problems does the virus cause?

A massive study shows how comparison groups shape findings about long COVID and which lasting health problems are linked to the virus.

Long COVID can leave people feeling unwell long after an infection. But figuring out which health problems the virus caused depends partly on who researchers compare those patients with.

A Stanford University team found just how much that choice matters.

When the researchers repeated an approach used in earlier studies, it linked COVID to unlikely problems, including injuries from lightning, drowning, and electrocution.

Changing the comparison group produced a much shorter list of lasting effects. By the second year, none met the study’s cutoff, though that does not mean every patient had recovered.

The team drew on 14.4 billion insurance claims from nearly 245 million US patients.

These are bills from doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies, so they record medical care rather than how someone feels each day.

Between about four months and a year after infection, the revised approach linked 98% fewer health problems to COVID than the older method did using the same records.

Jure Leskovec, a Stanford computer science professor, was one of the study’s senior authors.

“This doesn’t mean long COVID is 98 percent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID,” Leskovec said.

Many earlier studies compared people who tested positive with people who had no recorded COVID diagnosis. That second group included people who tested negative and people who never took a test.

Those groups may differ before COVID enters the picture. Someone might get tested during a visit for diabetes or another illness, or because they see doctors more often.

“If you compare people who tested positive for COVID with people who were never tested, you risk attributing differences in their underlying health and healthcare-seeking behavior to the virus itself,” Leskovec said.

The concern is that researchers could end up blaming COVID for problems linked to someone’s existing health or reasons for seeking care.

The team compared people who tested negative and never had COVID recorded with untested people who had similar medical histories.

Between one and four months later, 82.5% of the health problems tracked were at least 10% more common in the group that tested negative.

A negative test could not explain those extra problems; the researchers pointed to other factors associated with getting tested.

For the main analysis, follow-up began with each patient’s first PCR test between March 1, 2020, and March 1, 2021.

The team compared positive results only with negative results, so everyone had a reason to get tested.

The researchers then adjusted the comparison group to match the positive group’s medical history over the previous four years.

They also matched age, sex, and neighborhood measures such as income.

This matching approach is called a synthetic control. Co-senior author Stefan Wager, an associate professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business, said economists commonly use it.

The records came from Komodo Health, which gathers claims from insurers, pharmacies, and programs including Medicare and Medicaid.

The researchers followed patients for up to two years and examined 614 health outcomes.

“Even with 244 million patients, you can get highly precise answers to the wrong question. Study design matters as much as data size,” Leskovec said.

As an initial check, the revised method picked up familiar COVID symptoms during the first month of infection.

Hamed Nilforoshan, a Stanford computer science doctoral student and one of three first authors, also recreated the older approach, closely following a 2021 Nature study. “Something wasn’t adding up,” Nilforoshan said.

The team checked 49 outcomes that COVID could not plausibly cause, including firearm injuries and birth defects recorded in adults. The older approach linked COVID to more than half.

It suggested a 76% increase in a category of injuries that included lightning, drowning, and electrocution. It also suggested an 18.6% increase in adults receiving diagnoses for birth defects of the eye, ear, face, or neck.

The authors said chance or flaws in study design presumably explained those unlikely links.

The revised approach flagged just two of the 49 outcomes, both showing lower risk after a positive test, which suggests it may slightly underestimate some real effects.

For the main results, a health problem had to increase by at least 10% and pass a strict statistical check that accounted for hundreds of comparisons.

From day 30 to day 119, the revised method linked 43 health problems to COVID, compared with 262 under the older method.

From about four months to a year, the revised method found five, compared with 286 under the older method. In the second year, those counts were zero and 369.

On average, recorded health problems in the positive group fell to roughly the comparison group’s level within a year. Earlier US veterans studies had found harmful effects after two or three years.

During the first months, COVID remained linked to problems involving the lungs, heart and blood vessels, kidneys, immune system, muscles, gut, and nervous system. Hair loss also appeared.

The biggest relative increase involved myopathy, a muscle disease, with related insurance claims about three times as common after a positive test.

Hair loss claims were nearly twice as common, while palpitations, malnutrition, and fatigue were 12% to 21% more common.

Between about four months and a year, five problems still met the cutoff: myopathy, hair loss, two categories of blood clots in the lungs, and respiratory failure.

Pneumonia, shortness of breath, chest pain, and fatigue increased by less than 10%. Even small increases in such common problems can affect many people.

Steven Goodman, a professor in Stanford Medicine’s Department of Epidemiology and Population Health, compared the findings with illnesses that linger after other infections.

“These findings indicate that long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought,” Goodman said.

Still, billing records can miss symptoms such as fatigue and brain fog.

The study also covered people who sought PCR testing through healthcare, leaving out infections identified only through home tests.

About 20% of the comparison group caught COVID within two years, which could make the virus’s effects look smaller. The study could not establish what caused symptoms that lasted beyond a year.

The authors stressed that lasting symptoms are real. Other illnesses that prompted the original test, or other factors, could help explain them, but these records cannot settle that question.

“These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them,” Leskovec said.

The team called for research into the biology of long COVID and biomarkers, measurable signs in the body that could help identify it.

They also suggested repeating earlier studies with comparison groups based on testing to see how much their results change.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6400. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ
